b: Simple definition# A container is a normal Linux process that the kernel isolates — it gets its own view of files, network and processes, and limited CPU and memory. A container image is a portable package of the application and everything it needs (runtime, libraries, config defaults), built in layers and stored in a registry. Containers vs virtual machines# VMs virtualise hardware; containers virtualise the OS flowchart TB subgraph VM[&#34;Virtual machines&#34;] H1[&#34;Hardware&#34;] --&gt; HV[&#34;Hypervisor&#34;] HV --&gt; G1[&#34;Guest OS + app A&#34;] HV --&gt; G2[&#34;Guest OS + app B&#34;] end subgraph CT[&#34;Containers&#34;] H2[&#34;Hardware&#34;] --&gt; OS[&#34;Host OS kernel&#34;] OS --&gt; C1[&#34;Container: app A&lt;br/&gt;namespaces + cgroups&#34;] OS --&gt; C2[&#34;Container: app B&#34;] end VM Container Isolation Strong (separate kernel) Process-level (shared kernel) Start time Tens of seconds Milliseconds to seconds Size GBs MBs Density Lower Higher How it works# Namespaces isolate what a process sees: PID, network, mount, UTS (hostname), IPC, user. cgroups limit what it can use: CPU, memory, I/O. Union file systems stack read-only image layers with a thin writable layer. seccomp, capabilities, SELinux/AppArmor restrict what it may do. Images and OCI# Image layers flowchart TB L4[&#34;App JAR / binary — changes often&#34;] --&gt; L3[&#34;Dependencies&#34;] L3 --&gt; L2[&#34;Runtime: JRE, Python&#34;] L2 --&gt; L1[&#34;Base OS layer: distroless, UBI, Alpine&#34;] Layers are cached and shared — order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changed. The Open Container Initiative (OCI) standardises the image format, runtime and distribution, so images built with Docker, Buildah or Jib run on containerd, CRI-O or Podman. Registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, Quay, Harbor, ECR, ACR, Artifact Registry) also store Helm charts, SBOMs and signatures as OCI artifacts. A good Dockerfile# # ---- build stage ---- FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build WORKDIR /src COPY mvnw pom.xml ./ COPY .mvn .mvn RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline # cached unless pom.xml changes COPY src src RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests # ---- runtime stage ---- FROM gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12:nonroot WORKDIR /app COPY --from=build /src/target/app.jar app.jar USER nonroot EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT [&#34;java&#34;, &#34;-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75&#34;, &#34;-jar&#34;, &#34;app.jar&#34;] Best practices: Multi-stage builds — build tools stay out of the runtime image. Minimal, maintained base images — distroless, Chainguard, Docker Hardened Images (free since December 2025, with SBOMs and SLSA provenance), Red Hat UBI micro. Run as non-root; read-only root file system where possible. Pin base images by digest and rebuild regularly for patches. No secrets in images — use BuildKit secret mounts at build time and runtime secret injection. .dockerignore to keep the build context small. One process per container; log to stdout/stderr. JVM in containers: container-aware memory flags (MaxRAMPercentage); consider CDS/AOT or native images for start-up time. Build tools# Tool Notes Docker + BuildKit / buildx Default; multi-platform builds, cache export, SBOM and provenance attestations Buildah / Podman Daemonless, rootless; common on Red Hat platforms Kaniko / BuildKit in CI Build inside Kubernetes without a Docker daemon Jib (Java) Builds optimised layers without a Dockerfile Cloud Native Buildpacks (Paketo) Source to image with maintained base images; used by Spring Boot build-image Runtimes: Docker, containerd, Podman# Runtime stack flowchart TB CLI[&#34;docker CLI / podman / kubelet&#34;] --&gt; HL[&#34;High-level runtime&lt;br/&gt;containerd, CRI-O, Podman&#34;] HL --&gt; LL[&#34;Low-level OCI runtime&lt;br/&gt;runc, crun&#34;] LL --&gt; K[&#34;Linux kernel&lt;br/&gt;namespaces, cgroups&#34;] Docker Engine uses containerd internally; great for developer machines and builds. Docker Desktop adds Compose, Kubernetes and dev tooling. Kubernetes talks to containerd or CRI-O via CRI. (Kubernetes 1.35 is the last release supporting containerd 1.x — move to containerd 2.) Podman is daemonless and rootless, Docker-CLI compatible. Container security essentials# Scan images in CI and registries (Trivy, Grype, registry scanners); block critical CVEs with policy. Generate SBOMs, sign images (cosign), verify at admission — see Kubernetes security. Drop capabilities, non-root, seccomp; never --privileged. Keep images small and rebuild often. Common mistakes# Common mistakeUsing :latest Not reproducible and impossible to roll back reliably. Tag with version and deploy by digest. Common mistakeHuge images with build tools and shells Larger attack surface and slower pulls. Use multi-stage builds and minimal bases. Common mistakeBaking environment config and secrets into images Build once; inject configuration per environment at deploy time. Quick check# What isolates a container? Linux namespaces (what it can see) and cgroups (what it can use), plus seccomp, capabilities and LSMs (what it may do). Why use multi-stage builds? To keep compilers and build tools out of the runtime image, making it smaller and more secure. What is OCI? The Open Container Initiative standards for image format, runtime and distribution, which let images run on any compliant runtime. Docker vs containerd vs Podman? Docker is a developer platform built on containerd; containerd (and CRI-O) are runtimes used by Kubernetes via CRI; Podman is a daemonless, rootless Docker-compatible engine. Why deploy by digest? A digest identifies exact image content, so deployments are reproducible and cannot be changed by re-tagging. Summary# Containers are isolated processes; images are layered OCI packages. Multi-stage, minimal, non-root, pinned, secret-free images. Build with BuildKit, Buildah, Jib or Buildpacks; run on containerd/CRI-O. Scan, SBOM, sign and verify every image. References# Open Container Initiative. Docker, Best practices for building images. Docker,

b: Simple definition# Kubernetes is an open-source platform that runs containerised applications across a cluster of machines. You tell it what you want — &ldquo;run three copies of this image, reachable on port 8080&rdquo; — and it continuously works to make the cluster match, restarting, rescheduling and replacing containers as machines and workloads change. The problem it solves# Running containers on one server is easy. Running hundreds of services across hundreds of servers raises hard questions: Which machine has room? What happens when a machine dies? How do services find each other? How do you roll out a new version without downtime? Kubernetes answers these with a common API and automation, so teams do not script them by hand. The core idea: declarative state and reconciliation# The reconciliation loop every controller runs flowchart LR D[&#34;Desired state&lt;br/&gt;spec in etcd&#34;] --&gt; C{&#34;Controller compares&#34;} A[&#34;Actual state&lt;br/&gt;status from the cluster&#34;] --&gt; C C --&gt;|&#34;different&#34;| ACT[&#34;Act: create, delete,&lt;br/&gt;update objects&#34;] ACT --&gt; A C --&gt;|&#34;same&#34;| W[&#34;Wait for next change&#34;] W --&gt; C Every object has a spec (what you want) and a status (what is). Controllers watch objects through the API server and act to close the gap — forever, not once. This is why Kubernetes self-heals: delete a Pod managed by a Deployment and a new one appears, because desired state still says &ldquo;three replicas&rdquo;. Cluster architecture# Kubernetes cluster architecture · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Control plane# Component Role kube-apiserver The single front door. Every read and write goes through it. Performs authentication, authorisation and admission control, then stores objects in etcd. Stateless and horizontally scalable. etcd Consistent, distributed key-value store holding all cluster state. Uses the Raft consensus algorithm, so it needs an odd number of members (3 or 5) for quorum. Back it up. kube-scheduler Watches for Pods without a node, filters nodes that fit (resources, taints, affinity), scores them, and binds the Pod to the best node. kube-controller-manager Runs built-in controllers: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job, EndpointSlice, ServiceAccount and more. cloud-controller-manager Integrates with the cloud provider: load balancers for Services, node lifecycle, routes. Worker nodes# Component Role kubelet Agent on every node. Watches Pods assigned to its node, asks the runtime to start containers, runs probes, reports status. Container runtime Pulls images and runs containers through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) — typically containerd or CRI-O. (Docker Engine support via dockershim was removed in 1.24; images built with Docker still run.) kube-proxy Programs Service routing on the node (iptables or nftables). Many clusters replace it with an eBPF data plane such as Cilium. CNI plugin Gives each Pod an IP and connects Pod networks across nodes. See networking. What happens on kubectl apply# From apply to running containers sequenceDiagram participant U as kubectl participant API as kube-apiserver participant E as etcd participant DC as Deployment controller participant S as Scheduler participant K as kubelet participant R as containerd U-&gt;&gt;API: apply Deployment (replicas: 3) API-&gt;&gt;API: authenticate, authorise, admit API-&gt;&gt;E: store Deployment DC-&gt;&gt;API: watch: new Deployment DC-&gt;&gt;API: create ReplicaSet, then 3 Pods (no node) S-&gt;&gt;API: watch: unscheduled Pods S-&gt;&gt;API: bind each Pod to a node K-&gt;&gt;API: watch: Pod bound to my node K-&gt;&gt;R: pull image, start containers K-&gt;&gt;API: update Pod status: Running, Ready Notice that no component calls another directly — they all watch and update objects through the API server. This loose coupling is what makes Kubernetes extensible. Extending Kubernetes# Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) add new object types (for example Certificate, Application, PostgresCluster). Operators are custom controllers that reconcile CRDs — encoding operational knowledge (install, upgrade, back up a database) as code. Admission webhooks and policies validate or mutate objects (security). Aggregated APIs and the Gateway API, CSI, CNI, CRI standard interfaces let vendors plug in without forking Kubernetes. High availability# Highly available control plane flowchart TB LB[&#34;Load balancer :6443&#34;] --&gt; A1[&#34;API server 1&lt;br/&gt;zone a&#34;] LB --&gt; A2[&#34;API server 2&lt;br/&gt;zone b&#34;] LB --&gt; A3[&#34;API server 3&lt;br/&gt;zone c&#34;] A1 --&gt; E1[(&#34;etcd 1&#34;)] A2 --&gt; E2[(&#34;etcd 2&#34;)] A3 --&gt; E3[(&#34;etcd 3&#34;)] E1 &lt;--&gt; E2 E2 &lt;--&gt; E3 E1 &lt;--&gt; E3 Three or five control-plane nodes across zones; etcd quorum survives the loss of one (of three) or two (of five) members. Scheduler and controller-manager run active/standby using leader election. Worker nodes spread across zones; workloads use topology spread constraints and PodDisruptionBudgets. Managed Kubernetes (Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE, Red Hat OpenShift on cloud) runs the control plane for you — the default choice unless you have a strong reason to self-manage. Versions and upgrades# Kubernetes releases about three minor versions a year (1.34 in August 2025, 1.35 in December 2025, 1.36 in April 2026); each is supported for roughly 14 months upstream. Upgrade one minor version at a time: control plane first, then nodes; read deprecation notes; test add-ons (CNI, ingress/gateway, CSI). Recent milestones architects should know: sidecar containers stable (1.33), in-place Pod resize stable (1.35), cgroup v1 support removed by default (1.35), Dynamic Resource Allocation for GPUs and accelerators maturing (stable core in 1.34, more in 1.36), user namespaces GA (1.36), and the retirement of the community ingress-nginx controller in March 2026 in favour of the Gateway

b: Simple definition# Platform engineering is the discipline of building and running internal platforms — curated, self-service capabilities for infrastructure, delivery, security and operations — so that application teams can deliver software quickly and safely without each team becoming an expert in Kubernetes, cloud, networking and compliance. Why it emerged# &ldquo;You build it, you run it&rdquo; DevOps gave teams ownership — and also gave every team the whole cloud native landscape to learn. The result: cognitive overload, duplicated tooling, inconsistent security and slow onboarding. From DevOps sprawl to a platform flowchart LR subgraph Before[&#34;Every team does everything&#34;] T1[&#34;Team A: own CI, clusters,&lt;br/&gt;secrets, monitoring&#34;] T2[&#34;Team B: different CI,&lt;br/&gt;different clusters&#34;] T3[&#34;Team C: tickets to ops&lt;br/&gt;for every resource&#34;] end subgraph After[&#34;Platform as a product&#34;] P[&#34;Platform team&lt;br/&gt;self-service APIs, golden paths,&lt;br/&gt;guardrails built in&#34;] A1[&#34;Team A&#34;] --&gt; P A2[&#34;Team B&#34;] --&gt; P A3[&#34;Team C&#34;] --&gt; P end Before --&gt; After Platform as a product# Product practice In a platform team Know your users Interview developers; map their journeys and pain points Product manager A platform product owner prioritises by developer value Roadmap Published; built with users Adoption is voluntary The paved road must be easier than the alternatives Measure outcomes Adoption, onboarding time, lead time, satisfaction — not number of tools Documentation &amp; support Docs, examples, office hours, SLOs for the platform itself Team Topologies# Team Topologies flowchart TB SA[&#34;Stream-aligned teams&lt;br/&gt;deliver business value&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;X-as-a-Service&#34;| PT[&#34;Platform team&lt;br/&gt;self-service capabilities&#34;] EN[&#34;Enabling team&lt;br/&gt;coaching, adoption&#34;] -.-&gt;|&#34;facilitating&#34;| SA CS[&#34;Complicated-subsystem team&lt;br/&gt;e.g. payments engine, ML models&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;X-as-a-Service&#34;| SA Stream-aligned teams own a product or value stream end to end. Platform teams reduce their cognitive load by offering internal services. Enabling teams help others adopt practices (SRE, security, testing). Interaction modes: collaboration (temporary), X-as-a-Service (default for platforms), facilitating. Golden paths and guardrails# A golden path (or paved road) is an opinionated, supported, end-to-end way to do a common task — &ldquo;create a new Java service&rdquo;, &ldquo;add a Postgres database&rdquo;, &ldquo;expose an API&rdquo; — with security, observability and compliance built in. Optional, not mandatory: teams may leave the path, but then own the extra work. Guardrails, not gates: policies enforced automatically (admission, scans, budgets) instead of manual reviews. Living code: templates are versioned and updated; existing services get upgrades (for example via Renovate or template updates). The thinnest viable platform# Start with the smallest thing that removes the biggest pain — sometimes a wiki page with standards and a few templates. Grow the platform from real demand rather than building a large platform up front. Platform capabilities# Capability area Examples Developer portal Catalog, docs, templates, scorecards (Backstage) Delivery CI templates, registries, GitOps, progressive delivery Runtime Kubernetes clusters, namespaces, gateways, service mesh Infrastructure self-service Databases, queues, buckets via Crossplane/kro/Terraform modules Security Identity, secrets, policies, image signing, scanning Observability OpenTelemetry, dashboards, alerting, SLO tooling Cost Allocation, showback, budgets AI capabilities Model gateways, GPU pools, MCP servers, AI-assisted golden paths CNCF platform maturity model# The CNCF Platforms working group&rsquo;s maturity model assesses five aspects across four levels (provisional → operational → scalable → optimizing): Aspect Question Investment How are staff and funds allocated to the platform? Adoption How and why do users discover and use it? Interfaces How do users interact with it (tickets → self-service → APIs and portals)? Operations How are capabilities planned, run and maintained? Measurement How is feedback gathered and used? Roles in a platform team# Platform product manager, platform engineers (Kubernetes, cloud, delivery), SRE, security engineers, developer advocates / technical writers. Size grows with adoption — measured by value delivered, not ticket throughput. Platform engineering and AI (2026)# AI-assisted golden paths: natural-language requests that produce repositories, manifests and pipelines from approved templates. Platforms for AI workloads: GPU pools, DRA scheduling, model serving, AI gateways — industry surveys in 2026 show many organisations integrating AI workloads into existing developer platforms rather than building separate ones. Agents as platform users: coding agents consume the same APIs, templates and guardrails (for example via MCP servers), so the platform&rsquo;s guardrails protect against agent mistakes too. Common mistakes# Common mistakeBuilding a platform nobody asked for A big-bang platform designed without users gets bypassed. Start thin, co-design with pilot teams and measure adoption. Common mistakeRenaming the ops team &ldquo;platform&rdquo; without changing the model If the interface is still tickets, it is not a platform. Aim for self-service APIs and portals. Building and running internal self-service platforms that reduce developers&rsquo; cognitive load and embed security, reliability and compliance. What does &ldquo;platform as a product&rdquo; mean? b: Answers are short — enough to check your understanding. Each section links to the articles with full explanations. TipHow to use this page Cover the answer, explain it in your own words, then compare. Mark anything you hesitated on and reread the linked article. Aim for 80% before moving on. 1. Kubernetes architecture# Read: Kubernetes architecture. What does &ldquo;declarative&rdquo; mean in Kubernetes? You store desired state as API objects; controllers continuously reconcile actual state toward it. Which component is the only one that talks to etcd? The kube-apiserver. What do the scheduler and the kubelet each do? The scheduler assigns Pods to nodes; the kubelet on each node runs the assigned Pods through the container runtime and reports status. Why 3 or 5 etcd members? Raft needs a majority for quorum; odd sizes maximise tolerated failures (1 of 3, 2 of 5). What is a CRD and an operator? A CRD adds a new API type; an operator is a controller that reconciles it to automate an application&rsquo;s lifecycle. What runtime interfaces does Kubernetes use? CRI (runtimes), CNI (networking), CSI (storage). How often does Kubernetes release, and how should you upgrade? About three minor releases a year; upgrade one minor version at a time, control plane before nodes. 2. Workloads, scheduling and storage# Read: Workloads &amp; scheduling. Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet? Stateless replicas; stable identity with per-Pod storage; one Pod per node. Readiness vs liveness vs startup probes? Readiness gates traffic; liveness restarts stuck containers; startup delays other probes until the app has started. What happens when a container exceeds memory vs CPU limits? Memory: OOM-killed. CPU: throttled. What are the QoS classes? Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort. What do taints and tolerations do? Taints repel Pods from nodes; only Pods with matching tolerations may be scheduled there. HPA vs KEDA vs VPA vs Karpenter? Replicas on metrics; replicas on events including scale to zero; right-sizing requests; node provisioning and consolidation. What chain provides persistent storage? PVC → StorageClass → CSI driver → PersistentVolume. What is in-place Pod resize? Changing CPU and memory of running containers without restarting the Pod — stable since Kubernetes 1.35. 3. Networking and service mesh# Read: Networking, Service mesh. What does a CNI plugin do? Assigns Pod IPs and connects Pods across nodes according to the network model. Why do Services exist? To provide stable virtual IPs and DNS names for changing sets of Pods. Name the Service types. ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, headless, ExternalName. What are the Gateway API&rsquo;s main resources? GatewayClass, Gateway, and routes such as HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute. What happened to ingress-nginx in 2026? The community controller was retired in March 2026; migrate to the Gateway API or a maintained controller. How do you isolate a namespace&rsquo;s network? Default-deny NetworkPolicy plus explicit allows, including DNS. What does a service mesh add? mTLS identity, traffic management, resilience features and telemetry without code changes. What are ztunnel and waypoints? In Istio ambient mode: a per-node L4 mTLS proxy, and optional L7 proxies where needed. 4. Kubernetes security# Read: Kubernetes security. What are the 4Cs? Cloud, cluster, container, code. Which three checks does every API request pass? Authentication, authorisation (RBAC) and admission control. What does Pod Security &ldquo;restricted&rdquo; require? Non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, seccomp RuntimeDefault, no host namespaces. Kyverno, Gatekeeper or ValidatingAdmissionPolicy? Kyverno — YAML policies incl. mutation and image verification; Gatekeeper — Rego; VAP — built-in CEL rules without webhooks. Why aren&rsquo;t Secrets secure by default? They are base64-encoded; use etcd encryption at rest, RBAC and external secret stores. What secures the supply chain? Minimal images, scanning, SBOMs, SLSA provenance, cosign signatures and verification at admission; deploy by digest. What is workload identity? Mapping Kubernetes service accounts to cloud IAM roles so Pods get short-lived cloud credentials without stored keys. 5. Containers, Kubernetes operations and OpenShift# Read: Containers &amp; Docker, Kubernetes in practice, OpenShift. What isolates a container? Namespaces, cgroups, and security mechanisms (seccomp, capabilities, LSMs). Why multi-stage builds? Smaller, safer runtime images without build tools. Docker vs containerd vs Podman? Developer platform built on containerd; Kubernetes runtime via CRI; daemonless rootless engine. Kustomize vs Helm? Overlay patches for your own YAML vs versioned, templated packages. What is Cluster API? Declarative lifecycle management of Kubernetes clusters. What does OpenShift add to Kubernetes? An integrated supported platform: RHCOS, CRI-O, SCCs, Routes, OLM, Pipelines (Tekton), GitOps (Argo CD), Service Mesh, Virtualization, Developer Hub. What is an SCC? A Security Context Constraint controlling Pod privileges in OpenShift. 6. Helm, CI/CD, GitOps and release orchestration# Read: Helm, CI/CD, GitOps, Release orchestration. Chart vs values vs release? Template package; configuration; installed instance with history. Name three Helm 4 changes. Server-side apply by default for new releases, WebAssembly plugins, install by digest (also renamed flags, kstatus waiting). Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment? Every change releasable vs every passing change released automatically. Why build once and promote? The tested artifact is the released artifact. Blue-green vs canary? Full switch between two environments vs gradual traffic shift with analysis. Name the DORA metrics. Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, failed deployment recovery time. What are the OpenGitOps principles? Declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled. Argo CD vs Flux? Argo CD: UI,

b: Simple definition# Site reliability engineering (SRE) applies software engineering to operations. Its central idea: decide how reliable a service needs to be (a Service Level Objective), measure it, and use the gap between 100% and the objective — the error budget — to balance reliability work against feature delivery. SLI, SLO, SLA# Term Meaning Example SLI — indicator A measurement of user-visible behaviour % of /checkout requests that succeed within 300 ms SLO — objective Target for an SLI over a window 99.9% over 28 days SLA — agreement A contract with consequences 99.5% monthly, or service credits Set SLOs stricter than SLAs so you act before breaching contracts. Not every service needs an SLA; every important service needs SLOs. Good SLIs# Service type SLIs Request/response (APIs, web) Availability (good / valid requests), latency (requests faster than threshold) Data pipelines Freshness, completeness, correctness Storage Durability, availability of reads/writes Measure as close to the user as possible (load balancer or gateway, synthetic checks, real-user monitoring), as a ratio of good events / valid events. Error budgets# Error budget = 1 − SLO. A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of full unavailability (or the equivalent in failed requests). SLO Allowed downtime per 30 days 99% ~7.2 hours 99.5% ~3.6 hours 99.9% ~43 minutes 99.95% ~22 minutes 99.99% ~4.3 minutes Error budget policy (agreed with product owners): while budget remains, ship features; when it is exhausted, prioritise reliability work and slow risky releases. Burn-rate alerting# Alert when the budget is being consumed too fast, not on every error spike: Alert Condition (for a 99.9% SLO) Meaning Page (fast burn) Burn rate ≥ 14.4 over 1 h and 5 min 2% of the monthly budget gone in an hour Page (medium) Burn rate ≥ 6 over 6 h and 30 min 5% in six hours Ticket (slow burn) Burn rate ≥ 1 over 3 days On track to exhaust the budget Multi-window conditions reduce false alarms and still detect fast incidents. Tools such as Sloth, Pyrra or OpenSLO definitions generate these rules for Prometheus. Toil and automation# Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales with load and has no lasting value (restarting pods, manual certificate renewals, provisioning by ticket). SRE teams cap toil (Google&rsquo;s guideline: under 50% of time) and automate it away — often by building it into the platform. Incident management# Incident lifecycle · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Roles# Role Responsibility Incident commander Owns coordination and decisions; does not debug Operations / technical lead Investigates and mitigates Communications lead Status page, stakeholders, executives Scribe Timeline of events and decisions Principles# Mitigate first (roll back, fail over, scale, disable a feature flag), find root cause later. Declare incidents early; it is cheap to downgrade. Use severity levels with clear criteria (user impact, revenue, data, security). Communicate on a cadence, even when there is no news. Blameless postmortems# A postmortem records impact, timeline, contributing factors, what went well, and owned, prioritised actions. &ldquo;Blameless&rdquo; means focusing on systems and decisions given the information available — people should feel safe to share details, or you will never learn the real causes. On-call that is sustainable# Alerts must be actionable and tied to SLOs; delete noisy alerts. Runbooks linked from every alert. Rotations of 5–8 people; follow-the-sun where possible; compensation and recovery time. Track pages per shift; &gt; 2 incidents per shift is a reliability signal, not a staffing one. SRE in a platform organisation# SRE engagement models flowchart LR A[&#34;Embedded SRE&lt;br/&gt;in product teams&#34;] --- B[&#34;Platform SRE&lt;br/&gt;reliability of the platform itself&#34;] B --- C[&#34;Consulting / enabling SRE&lt;br/&gt;SLO workshops, reviews&#34;] Platform teams bake SRE practices into golden paths: default SLOs and dashboards per service template, burn-rate alerts, runbook templates and incident tooling. Common mistakes# Common mistake100% as the target Unachievable and paralysing: every change becomes risky. Users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% through their own networks. Common mistakeAlerting on causes (CPU 80%) Page on symptoms users feel (SLO burn); use causes for dashboards and diagnosis. Common mistakePostmortems without follow-through Actions without owners or deadlines repeat the incident. Track them like product work. Quick check# What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA? An SLI measures user-visible behaviour; an SLO is the target for it; an SLA is a contractual commitment with consequences, set looser than the SLO. How much downtime does a 99.9% SLO allow per 30 days? About 43 minutes. What is an error budget policy? An agreement on what happens as budget is consumed — ship freely while budget remains; prioritise reliability and slow risky changes when it is exhausted. Why alert on burn rate instead of error rate? Burn rate relates errors to the SLO, alerting only when the budget is threatened; multi-window conditions catch fast and slow burns with fewer false alarms. What does the incident commander do? Coordinates the response, assigns roles, makes decisions and manages communication — without doing the hands-on debugging. What is toil? Manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales with load and has no lasting value. Summary# Define SLIs close to users; set SLOs; derive error budgets and policies. Alert on multi-window burn rates; keep alerts actionable. Run incidents with clear roles; mitigate first; blameless postmortems with owned actions. Eliminate toil; build SRE defaults into the platform. References# Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, O&rsquo;Reilly, 2016, and The SRE Workbook, 2018 (chapter &ldquo;Alerting on SLOs&rdquo;). OpenSLO. PagerDuty, Incident Response documentation.

b: Simple definition# An internal developer platform (IDP) is the sum of tools, APIs, templates and automation that a platform team integrates into self-service golden paths. A developer portal (such as Backstage) is the front door to the IDP — but the portal is not the platform; the automation behind it is. Reference architecture# Internal developer platform reference architecture · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Plane Purpose Typical tools Developer control plane Where developers interact: portal, CLI, IDE, templates, docs Backstage / Red Hat Developer Hub, Port, Cortex; IDE plug-ins Integration &amp; delivery Build, store and deliver artifacts GitHub Actions, GitLab, Tekton; OCI registries; Argo CD, Flux; Argo Rollouts Resource plane Run workloads and provision infrastructure Kubernetes, cloud services; Crossplane, kro, Terraform/OpenTofu modules; platform orchestrators Observability plane Telemetry and SLOs OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, tracing backends Security plane Identity, secrets, policy, supply chain Vault, External Secrets, Kyverno/OPA, Sigstore, scanners The developer portal: Backstage# Backstage, created at Spotify and now a CNCF project, is the most widely used portal framework. Backstage building blocks flowchart LR CAT[&#34;Software Catalog&lt;br/&gt;services, APIs, teams, resources&lt;br/&gt;from catalog-info.yaml&#34;] --&gt; P[&#34;Portal&#34;] TPL[&#34;Software Templates&lt;br/&gt;scaffolder: new service, new DB&#34;] --&gt; P DOC[&#34;TechDocs&lt;br/&gt;docs-as-code&#34;] --&gt; P SC[&#34;Scorecards / tech insights&lt;br/&gt;standards, maturity&#34;] --&gt; P PLUG[&#34;Plugins&lt;br/&gt;Kubernetes, Argo CD, CI, cost, PagerDuty&#34;] --&gt; P # catalog-info.yaml in every repository apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1 kind: Component metadata: name: orders description: Order management service annotations: argocd/app-name: orders-prod backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:. spec: type: service lifecycle: production owner: team-shop system: checkout providesApis: [orders-api] dependsOn: [resource:orders-db] Software catalog — ownership, dependencies and metadata for every service, API and resource: the backbone for incident response, security and cost. Software templates — golden paths that create repos, CI, manifests and catalog entries. TechDocs — Markdown docs next to code, rendered in the portal. Plugins — show Kubernetes status, Argo CD sync, pipelines, alerts and cost per service. Options: self-host Backstage (needs a team to maintain), Red Hat Developer Hub (supported Backstage), managed Backstage (Roadie), or alternative portals (Port, Cortex, OpsLevel). Infrastructure as APIs# Developers should request capabilities (&ldquo;a Postgres database for orders, prod size&rdquo;) rather than raw cloud resources. Composition: a claim becomes real infrastructure flowchart LR CLAIM[&#34;Claim (team namespace)&lt;br/&gt;kind: Database&lt;br/&gt;size: medium, engine: postgres&#34;] --&gt; XRD[&#34;Platform API&lt;br/&gt;Crossplane XRD / kro ResourceGraph&#34;] XRD --&gt; COMP[&#34;Composition&lt;br/&gt;platform team&#39;s recipe&#34;] COMP --&gt; R1[&#34;Cloud SQL / RDS instance&lt;br/&gt;encrypted, backups, private network&#34;] COMP --&gt; R2[&#34;Secret via External Secrets&#34;] COMP --&gt; R3[&#34;Monitoring + alerts&#34;] Tool Approach Crossplane Kubernetes control plane for infrastructure; Composite Resource Definitions + Compositions; providers for every cloud kro (Kube Resource Orchestrator) Define custom APIs that group Kubernetes resources (including cloud controller resources) into a graph Terraform / OpenTofu modules Mature IaC; exposed via templates, pipelines or operators Platform orchestrators (for example Humanitec) Generate environment-specific config from a workload spec (Score) and rules Golden path in action# The developer platform case study shows the full flow: a developer picks a template, the platform creates the repository and pipeline, provisions a namespace and database through claims, and Argo CD deploys the first version — in minutes, without tickets. Reference stacks# CNOE (Cloud Native Operational Excellence) — an industry initiative publishing open-source reference implementations (Backstage + Argo CD + Crossplane + Argo Workflows + Keycloak and more). Cloud provider platforms — opinionated combinations on EKS, AKS, GKE. OpenShift — integrated delivery, GitOps and Developer Hub (OpenShift). Build, buy or assemble?# Option Pros Cons Assemble open source (Backstage, Argo CD, Crossplane) Flexible, no licence Needs a strong platform team Commercial portals / orchestrators Faster value, support Cost, vendor fit Integrated platform (OpenShift + Developer Hub) One vendor, integrated Less choice, licence Most enterprises assemble around a few strategic open-source components and buy where differentiation is low. Common mistakes# Common mistakePortal first, platform later A beautiful catalog with no automation behind it is a documentation site. Build the golden paths and APIs; the portal surfaces them. Common mistakeExposing raw cloud resources Developers then need cloud expertise again. Expose capabilities with sensible defaults and policies. Common mistakeAn incomplete catalog If ownership data is missing, incident response and cost allocation fail. Make catalog registration part of every template. Quick check# What is the difference between an IDP and a developer portal? The IDP is the platform — tools, APIs, automation and golden paths; the portal is its user interface. Name the five planes of an IDP reference architecture. Developer control plane, integration and delivery, resource, observability and security planes. What are Backstage&rsquo;s core features? Software catalog, software templates (scaffolder), TechDocs and a plugin ecosystem (plus scorecards via plugins). What does Crossplane do? d: IDP reference architecture planes (developer control plane, integration and delivery, resources, observability, security), the developer portal with Backstage (catalog, software templates, TechDocs, scorecards), platform orchestrators and infrastructure APIs (Crossplane, kro, Terraform), golden-path flows, build vs buy, and CNOE reference stacks.

b: Simple definition# &ldquo;Running Kubernetes&rdquo; covers day 1 (creating clusters and deploying apps) and day 2 (upgrading, scaling, securing, backing up and operating them for years). Most of the cost and risk of Kubernetes is in day 2. A minimal application# apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: { name: orders, namespace: shop, labels: { app: orders } } spec: replicas: 3 selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders } } template: metadata: { labels: { app: orders } } spec: containers: - name: orders image: ghcr.io/acme/orders@sha256:3f1c... # deploy by digest ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }] resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi } limits: { memory: 512Mi } readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } } livenessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 } } --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: { name: orders, namespace: shop } spec: selector: { app: orders } ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }] --- apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: HTTPRoute metadata: { name: orders, namespace: shop } spec: parentRefs: [{ name: public, namespace: gateway }] hostnames: [&#34;shop.example.com&#34;] rules: - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /orders } }] backendRefs: [{ name: orders, port: 80 }] kubectl essentials# Task Command Apply desired state kubectl apply -f k8s/ (or server-side: --server-side) See what changes kubectl diff -f k8s/ Inspect kubectl get pods -n shop -o wide, kubectl describe pod &lt;p&gt; Logs kubectl logs deploy/orders -f --since=10m Debug kubectl debug -it &lt;pod&gt; --image=busybox --target=orders (ephemeral container) Rollout kubectl rollout status deploy/orders, kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders Events kubectl events -n shop --types=Warning Permissions kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n shop --as=jane In production, humans should rarely apply by hand — use GitOps. Managing configuration: Kustomize vs Helm# Kustomize overlays flowchart TB B[&#34;base/&lt;br/&gt;deployment, service, route&#34;] --&gt; D[&#34;overlays/dev&lt;br/&gt;1 replica, dev image&#34;] B --&gt; S[&#34;overlays/staging&lt;br/&gt;2 replicas&#34;] B --&gt; P[&#34;overlays/prod&lt;br/&gt;3 replicas, HPA, PDB&#34;] Kustomize Helm Approach Patch plain YAML (overlays) Templates + values Packaging/distribution No Charts in OCI registries, versioned Best for Your own apps, environment differences Reusable, distributable packages; third-party software Built into kubectl Yes (kubectl apply -k) No Many teams combine them: Helm for third-party charts, Kustomize for internal apps — both rendered by Argo CD or Flux. See Helm. Operators# Operators run complex software on Kubernetes by encoding operational knowledge in a controller: Operator pattern flowchart LR CR[&#34;Custom resource&lt;br/&gt;PostgresCluster: 3 instances, v16, backups daily&#34;] --&gt; OP[&#34;Operator controller&#34;] OP --&gt; K[&#34;StatefulSets, Services,&lt;br/&gt;Secrets, backups, failover&#34;] K --&gt;|&#34;status&#34;| CR Use mature operators for databases (CloudNativePG, Crunchy), Kafka (Strimzi), certificates (cert-manager), monitoring (Prometheus Operator). Assess maturity (capability levels: install → upgrade → lifecycle → insights → autopilot) before trusting critical data to one. Managed or self-managed?# Option Examples Fit Managed Kubernetes Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE (incl. Autopilot) Default for cloud workloads Enterprise distributions Red Hat OpenShift, SUSE Rancher, VMware VKS Hybrid/on-premises, integrated platform, vendor support Lightweight k3s, k0s, Talos Edge, labs, small footprints DIY (kubeadm) — Rarely justified; maximum effort How many clusters?# Pattern Pros Cons Few large shared clusters Efficient, fewer upgrades Larger blast radius; noisy neighbours; complex tenancy Cluster per environment (dev/test/prod) Clear separation Still shared between teams Cluster per team or app Strong isolation, autonomy Many clusters to upgrade and secure Cluster per region/zone group Resilience, data residency Needs fleet management Most enterprises land on per-environment and per-region clusters shared by teams, with dedicated clusters for regulated or special workloads — managed as a fleet. Fleet management and lifecycle# Cluster API — Kubernetes-style declarative management of clusters themselves (create, upgrade, scale) across clouds. GitOps across the fleet — Argo CD ApplicationSets or Flux with cluster labels to roll out add-ons consistently. Upgrades — one minor version at a time; test add-ons; use surge node pools or blue/green node pools; respect PodDisruptionBudgets. Backup and restore — Velero (objects + volume snapshots); etcd snapshots for self-managed control planes; rebuild from Git for stateless config. Capacity — node pools by workload type (general, memory, GPU, spot); autoscaling (Karpenter / Cluster Autoscaler). Common mistakes# Common mistakeSnowflake clusters built by hand Clusters must be reproducible from code (Terraform/OpenTofu, Cluster API, GitOps). Otherwise recovery and upgrades become guesswork. Common mistakeOne giant cluster for everything A single misconfiguration or upgrade problem affects every team. Balance efficiency with blast radius. Quick check# Kustomize or Helm? Kustomize for patching your own YAML per environment; Helm for packaging and distributing reusable, versioned charts — often both, rendered by GitOps. What is an operator? A controller plus CRDs that automates the lifecycle of complex software, such as a database&rsquo;s provisioning, upgrades, backups and failover. Why prefer managed Kubernetes? The provider operates the control plane, etcd and upgrades, reducing operational risk and effort. How do you back up a cluster? Keep configuration in Git, use Velero for objects and volume snapshots, back up etcd for self-managed control planes, and regularly test restores. What is Cluster API? A Kubernetes project that manages the lifecycle of clusters declaratively, using Kubernetes
d: Day-1 and day-2 Kubernetes for architects: manifests and kubectl essentials, Kustomize overlays, operators, managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE) vs self-managed, cluster topology choices, upgrades, backup with Velero, and fleet management with Cluster API.

b: Simple definition# Monitoring tells you whether known things are wrong (dashboards and alerts on predefined metrics). Observability lets you ask why — including questions you did not anticipate — by exploring rich, correlated telemetry: metrics, logs, traces and increasingly profiles. The signals# Signal Answers Example Metrics How much / how often, over time? Cheap, aggregatable http_server_request_duration_seconds histogram Logs What exactly happened in this component? Structured JSON with trace ID Traces Where did time go across services for one request? Spans: gateway → orders → payments → DB Profiles Which code uses CPU/memory? Continuous profiling flame graphs Events What changed? Deployments, config changes, Kubernetes events Correlation is the superpower: a latency alert (metric) → an exemplar trace → the slow span → logs with the same trace ID → the profile for that service — in a few clicks. Methods for what to measure# RED (for services): Rate, Errors, Duration. USE (for resources): Utilisation, Saturation, Errors. Golden signals (Google SRE): latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Plus SLIs from SRE fundamentals. OpenTelemetry# OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for generating, collecting and exporting telemetry. It became a CNCF graduated project in 2026. Component Role API &amp; SDKs Instrument code in Java, Go, Python, .NET, JS and more Auto-instrumentation Java agent, zero-code instrumentation; the OTel Operator injects it into Pods Semantic conventions Standard attribute names (http.request.method, k8s.pod.name, gen_ai.*) OTLP The wire protocol for all signals Collector Receive, process (batch, sample, redact, enrich) and export to any backend Status (2026): traces, metrics and logs are stable; declarative configuration reached 1.0; profiles entered public alpha — promising but not yet for critical use. Reference pipeline on Kubernetes# OpenTelemetry pipeline on Kubernetes · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Sources — services instrumented with OTel SDKs or auto-instrumentation; nodes and Kubernetes (kubelet, cAdvisor, kube-state-metrics, eBPF). Collector agent (DaemonSet) on every node — receives OTLP, scrapes, adds Kubernetes metadata. Collector gateway (Deployment) — tail sampling, PII redaction, routing, rate limiting. Backends — metrics (Prometheus, Mimir, Thanos, VictoriaMetrics), logs (Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch), traces (Tempo, Jaeger), or commercial platforms. Use — Grafana dashboards, SLOs and burn-rate alerts to on-call. Prometheus essentials# Pull model: Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints discovered via Kubernetes service discovery or ServiceMonitors (Prometheus Operator). PromQL for queries and alert rules; Alertmanager routes and deduplicates alerts. Long-term, multi-cluster storage: Thanos, Mimir, Cortex or managed Prometheus services. # p95 latency per route over 5 minutes histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) eBPF-based observability# eBPF programs in the kernel capture network flows, latency and even HTTP/gRPC calls without code changes (Cilium Hubble, Pixie, Grafana Beyla, Coroot) and enable low-overhead continuous profiling. Great for coverage of uninstrumented services; combine with SDK instrumentation for business context. Cost and cardinality# Observability can become one of the largest platform costs. Cardinality: every unique label combination is a new time series. Never use user IDs, request IDs or unbounded values as metric labels. Sampling: head sampling (decide at start) or tail sampling in the Collector (keep errors and slow traces, sample the rest). Log levels and retention per environment; drop noisy logs at the Collector. Tiered storage and downsampling for old data. Logging practices# Structured JSON logs with timestamp, level, service, trace and span IDs. Log to stdout/stderr; let the platform collect. Never log secrets or unnecessary personal data; redact at the Collector. Common mistakes# Common mistakeDashboards for everything, alerts on causes Hundreds of dashboards nobody reads and pages on CPU. Alert on SLO burn; keep a few service and platform dashboards. Common mistakeVendor-specific instrumentation everywhere Switching vendors means re-instrumenting. Use OpenTelemetry and export where you like. Common mistakeUnbounded labels A user_id label can create millions of series and break the metrics backend. Quick check# What is the difference between monitoring and observability? Monitoring checks known conditions with predefined metrics and alerts; observability lets you explore correlated telemetry to answer new questions about why the system behaves as it does. Name the main telemetry signals. Metrics, logs, traces and profiles (plus events). What does the OpenTelemetry Collector do? Receives telemetry, processes it (batching, sampling, redaction, enrichment) and exports it to one or more backends. What are the RED and USE methods? RED — rate, errors, duration for services; USE — utilisation, saturation, errors for resources. What is high cardinality and why is it a problem? Too many unique label combinations creating huge numbers of time series, which increases cost and can overload metrics backends. What is tail sampling? Deciding which traces to keep after they complete — for example keeping all errors and slow traces and a fraction of the rest. Summary# Observability = correlated metrics, logs, traces and profiles to answer &ldquo;why&rdquo;. Instrument with OpenTelemetry; run Collector agents and gateways; export anywhere. Prometheus and Grafana-stack backends are common; eBPF fills coverage gaps. Control cardinality, sampling and retention; alert on SLOs. References# OpenTelemetry documentation and specification status. OpenTelemetry blog, Profiles enters public alpha, 2026. OpenTelemetry blog, OpenTelemetry has graduated, 2026. Prometheus documentation. Majors, Fong-Jones, Miranda,
d: Observability for cloud native systems: metrics, logs, traces and profiles; monitoring vs observability; the RED and USE methods; OpenTelemetry SDKs, Collector and semantic conventions; Prometheus and the Grafana stack; eBPF instrumentation; cardinality and cost; correlation; and a reference telemetry pipeline on Kubernetes.

b: How to use it# Use this checklist to review your own design before building, or a team&rsquo;s design at an architecture board or production-readiness review. Score each area 0–3 and record evidence. Nine review areas flowchart LR A1[&#34;1 · Goals &amp; SLOs&#34;] --&gt; A2[&#34;2 · Cluster topology&#34;] --&gt; A3[&#34;3 · Workloads&#34;] --&gt; A4[&#34;4 · Networking&#34;] --&gt; A5[&#34;5 · Security&#34;] A5 --&gt; A6[&#34;6 · Delivery&#34;] --&gt; A7[&#34;7 · Platform &amp; DevEx&#34;] --&gt; A8[&#34;8 · Observability &amp; resilience&#34;] --&gt; A9[&#34;9 · Cost &amp; operations&#34;] 1. Goals and SLOs# Business goals and users defined? SLOs, RTO and RPO per service tier? Red flags: &ldquo;five nines&rdquo; for everything; no owner per service. 2. Cluster topology# Managed or self-managed — and why? How many clusters, by environment/region/tenancy? Zones? Upgrade cadence and process? Clusters reproducible from code? Red flags: hand-built snowflake clusters; versions more than two minors behind; single-zone production. 3. Workloads# Requests/limits, probes, PDBs, topology spread, autoscaling for every production workload? Stateful services on managed databases or mature operators? Backups tested? Red flags: BestEffort Pods in prod; liveness probes that check dependencies; databases without tested restore. 4. Networking# Gateway API (not ingress-nginx); TLS everywhere; DNS automation? Default-deny NetworkPolicies; egress control; IP plan for growth? Service mesh justified? Red flags: one LoadBalancer per app; flat network; retired ingress controller. 5. Security# OIDC for humans; least-privilege RBAC; no cluster-admin for CI or apps? Pod Security restricted; policy as code enforced; secrets in an external store; workload identity? Signed images verified at admission; SBOMs; runtime detection; audit logs? Red flags: secrets in Git; :latest images; privileged Pods; shared admin kubeconfigs. 6. Delivery# Build once, promote by digest; DevSecOps scans; GitOps pull model? Progressive delivery with automated analysis and rollback? Database migration strategy? Change management automated with evidence; release orchestration where needed? Red flags: CI with production credentials; manual helm upgrade in prod; per-environment rebuilds. 7. Platform and developer experience# Golden paths for common tasks; catalog with owners; self-service infrastructure APIs? Platform run as a product with users, roadmap, metrics and SLOs? Red flags: ticket-driven provisioning; portal without automation; mandated tools nobody likes. 8. Observability and resilience# OpenTelemetry instrumentation; metrics, logs, traces correlated; SLO burn-rate alerts; runbooks? Timeouts, retries (one layer), circuit breakers; DR strategy per tier; drills; chaos experiments? Red flags: alerts on CPU only; no tracing; untested DR. 9. Cost and operations# Cost allocation by team (labels enforced); showback; budgets and anomaly alerts? Rightsizing, autoscaling, spot, commitments, non-prod schedules? On-call, incident process, postmortems, platform team capacity? Red flags: no cost visibility; requests far above usage; heroic on-call. Scoring rubric# Score Meaning 0 Missing 1 Mentioned, not designed 2 Designed with some gaps 3 Designed and evidenced (tests, numbers, prototypes, drills) Ready for production when no area is 0, security and resilience score 3 for Tier 0/1 services, and all gaps have owners and dates. One-page template# System / platform: Owner: Date: Reviewers: Decision requested: 1 Goals &amp; SLOs [0-3] Evidence / gaps: 2 Cluster topology [0-3] 3 Workloads [0-3] 4 Networking [0-3] 5 Security [0-3] 6 Delivery [0-3] 7 Platform &amp; DevEx [0-3] 8 Observability &amp; resilience [0-3] 9 Cost &amp; operations [0-3] Red flags: Conditions (owner, date): Decision: approve / approve with conditions / redesign Practice designs# Internal developer platform for 300 teams (worked example). Multi-region Kubernetes platform for a digital bank (worked example). Migrate 400 VMware VMs and 60 apps to Kubernetes/OpenShift within 18 months. A GPU platform on Kubernetes for 20 data-science teams. Replace a Jenkins + manual CAB release process with GitOps and automated change evidence. An edge platform for 2,000 retail stores running small clusters. Cut Kubernetes spend by 30% without hurting SLOs. Summary# Review nine areas from goals to cost; look for red flags; score with evidence. Approve with conditions and owners; re-review after major changes.
d: A repeatable checklist for reviewing Kubernetes and platform designs: nine review areas with questions and red flags, a 0–3 scoring rubric and a one-page review template.

b: Simple definition# A workload is an application running on Kubernetes. The smallest unit is a Pod — one or more containers that share a network identity and storage. You rarely create Pods directly; you use controllers (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) that create and manage Pods for you. Workload types# Which controller for which workload? flowchart TD Q{&#34;What kind of workload?&#34;} --&gt;|&#34;stateless service, web API&#34;| D[&#34;Deployment&lt;br/&gt;replicas, rolling updates&#34;] Q --&gt;|&#34;needs stable identity + own disk&lt;br/&gt;databases, Kafka&#34;| S[&#34;StatefulSet&lt;br/&gt;ordered, stable names, PVC per Pod&#34;] Q --&gt;|&#34;one per node&lt;br/&gt;log/metrics agents, CNI&#34;| DS[&#34;DaemonSet&#34;] Q --&gt;|&#34;run to completion&#34;| J[&#34;Job&lt;br/&gt;batch, migrations&#34;] Q --&gt;|&#34;on a schedule&#34;| CJ[&#34;CronJob&#34;] Object Key behaviour Pod Containers sharing IP, ports, volumes; ephemeral — replaced, never repaired Deployment Manages ReplicaSets; rolling update and rollback; for stateless apps StatefulSet Stable names (db-0, db-1), ordered start/stop, a PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod DaemonSet One Pod per (matching) node Job / CronJob Run until success; retries; schedules Init containers Run before app containers (setup, migrations) Sidecar containers Long-running helpers (proxies, log shippers) with proper start/stop ordering — stable since 1.33 Pod lifecycle and probes# Pod lifecycle with probes stateDiagram-v2 [*] --&gt; Pending: scheduled? image pulled? Pending --&gt; Running: containers started Running --&gt; Running: liveness fails → container restarted Running --&gt; Succeeded: all containers exit 0 Running --&gt; Failed: container exits non-zero, no restart Succeeded --&gt; [*] Failed --&gt; [*] Probe Question On failure Startup Has the app finished starting? Keep waiting (other probes disabled) until threshold, then restart Readiness Can it receive traffic now? Removed from Service endpoints (no restart) Liveness Is it stuck? Container restarted Common mistakeLiveness probes that check dependencies If the database is down and every Pod&rsquo;s liveness probe fails, Kubernetes restarts everything — making the outage worse. Liveness should check only the process itself; use readiness for dependency health. Resources: requests, limits and QoS# Request — what the scheduler reserves for the container; the basis of bin-packing and cost. Limit — the maximum. Exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed; exceeding CPU limit gets it throttled. QoS class Rule Eviction priority Guaranteed requests = limits for CPU and memory in every container Last Burstable Some requests set, not equal to limits Middle BestEffort No requests or limits First Practical defaults: always set memory requests and limits (equal for critical apps); set CPU requests; consider omitting CPU limits for latency-sensitive services to avoid throttling, while enforcing namespace quotas. In-place Pod resize (stable in 1.35) lets you change CPU and memory of running Pods without restarting them. Scheduling controls# Mechanism Use nodeSelector / node affinity Run on nodes with certain labels (GPU, zone, instance type) Pod affinity / anti-affinity Co-locate with, or keep apart from, other Pods Taints and tolerations Reserve nodes (for example GPU or system nodes); only tolerating Pods land there Topology spread constraints Spread replicas evenly across zones and nodes PriorityClass and preemption Important Pods can evict less important ones PodDisruptionBudget Limit voluntary disruptions (drains, upgrades) Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) Request GPUs and other devices with rich parameters; supports sharing and partitioning Autoscaling# The autoscaling layers flowchart TB L[&#34;Load rises&#34;] --&gt; HPA[&#34;HPA / KEDA&lt;br/&gt;more Pods&#34;] HPA --&gt; P{&#34;Pods pending?&lt;br/&gt;no room&#34;} P --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| NA[&#34;Node autoscaler&lt;br/&gt;Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter&lt;br/&gt;adds nodes&#34;] P --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| OK[&#34;Pods scheduled&#34;] NA --&gt; OK VPA[&#34;VPA / in-place resize&lt;br/&gt;right-size requests&#34;] -.-&gt; HPA Autoscaler Scales On HPA Replica count CPU, memory, custom/external metrics KEDA Replica count, including to zero Event sources: queue length, Kafka lag, cron, Prometheus queries VPA Requests/limits Observed usage (recommend, or apply — increasingly in place) Cluster Autoscaler Node groups Pending Pods; scale-down of idle nodes Karpenter Individual nodes, chosen to fit Pending Pods; consolidation to cheaper/fewer nodes; spot support Storage# Dynamic provisioning with CSI flowchart LR POD[&#34;Pod&#34;] --&gt; PVC[&#34;PersistentVolumeClaim&lt;br/&gt;10Gi, ReadWriteOnce&#34;] PVC --&gt; SC[&#34;StorageClass&lt;br/&gt;gp3, premium-ssd, ceph&#34;] SC --&gt; CSI[&#34;CSI driver&#34;] CSI --&gt; DISK[(&#34;Cloud disk / SAN / Ceph&#34;)] CSI --&gt; PV[&#34;PersistentVolume&lt;br/&gt;created and bound&#34;] PV --&gt; PVC PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) — what the app asks for. StorageClass — how to provision it. CSI driver — vendor plug-in that creates disks, snapshots and resizes. Access modes: ReadWriteOnce (one node), ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany (shared file systems), ReadWriteOncePod. Snapshots and volume group snapshots (stable in 1.36) for consistent backups; tools such as Velero back up objects and volumes. Stateful workloads: prefer managed databases; when running databases on Kubernetes, use mature operators (CloudNativePG, Strimzi for Kafka) and test failover and restore. Configuration# ConfigMaps for non-secret config; Secrets for credentials (base64, not encryption — enable etcd encryption and prefer external secret stores, see security). Namespaces separate teams and environments; ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges set budgets and defaults. Common mistakes# Common mistakeNo requests or limits BestEffort Pods are evicted first and make capacity planning and cost allocation impossible. Set requests on
d: Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs; probes and the Pod lifecycle; requests, limits and QoS; scheduling with affinity, taints and topology spread; HPA, VPA, KEDA, Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter; persistent volumes, CSI and stateful workloads.

b: Simple definition# Developer experience (DevEx) is how developers feel about, think about and value their work environment — tools, processes, platforms and culture. Good DevEx lets developers spend their time on valuable work instead of waiting, searching and fighting friction. It is the main outcome a platform team should improve. The three dimensions of DevEx# DevEx core dimensions flowchart TB DX[&#34;Developer experience&#34;] --&gt; FL[&#34;Feedback loops&lt;br/&gt;how fast do I learn if my change works?&lt;br/&gt;build, test, review, deploy times&#34;] DX --&gt; CL[&#34;Cognitive load&lt;br/&gt;how much do I need to know and hold in mind?&lt;br/&gt;tools, docs, complexity&#34;] DX --&gt; FS[&#34;Flow state&lt;br/&gt;can I focus without interruption?&lt;br/&gt;meetings, context switches, on-call&#34;] Inner loop and outer loop# Where developer time goes flowchart LR subgraph Inner[&#34;Inner loop — seconds to minutes&#34;] E[&#34;Edit&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Build&#34;] --&gt; T[&#34;Test locally&#34;] --&gt; E end subgraph Outer[&#34;Outer loop — minutes to days&#34;] PR[&#34;Pull request&#34;] --&gt; CI[&#34;CI&#34;] --&gt; RV[&#34;Review&#34;] --&gt; DEP[&#34;Deploy&#34;] --&gt; OBS[&#34;Observe in prod&#34;] end Inner --&gt; PR Platform teams improve both: fast local environments (dev containers, Tilt/Skaffold, remote dev environments, ephemeral preview environments) and a fast, reliable outer loop (CI speed, review tooling, GitOps, self-service). Measurement frameworks# Framework What it measures Notes DORA Delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, recovery time (+ reliability) System metrics; team/organisation level SPACE Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication &amp; collaboration, Efficiency &amp; flow A lens: use several dimensions, never one metric DevEx framework Feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state — perceptions + workflows Combines surveys and system data DX Core 4 Speed, effectiveness, quality, impact Unifies DORA, SPACE and DevEx into a small set Combine perception and system data# Type Examples Survey (perceptual) &ldquo;How easy is it to deploy a change?&rdquo; &ldquo;How often are you blocked waiting for other teams?&rdquo; Satisfaction with CI, docs, environments System (behavioural) CI duration and flakiness, PR review time, time to first deploy for a new service, environment provisioning time, incident load Platform-specific metrics# Metric Why Time to first deploy for a new service End-to-end golden path effectiveness Onboarding time to first merged PR Docs, access, environments Golden path adoption % of services on templates, current versions Self-service rate Requests fulfilled without tickets Platform NPS / satisfaction Product health Platform reliability SLOs of CI, registry, GitOps, clusters Common mistakeMeasuring individuals by activity Lines of code, commits or story points per person encourage gaming and damage trust. Measure systems and teams, combine with surveys, and use data to remove friction — not to rank people. AI coding assistants and agents# Assistants and coding agents can shorten the inner loop, but gains depend on context: codebase knowledge, review capacity, tests and CI speed. Measure impact with the same frameworks: lead time, change failure rate, review load, developer satisfaction — not &ldquo;lines of AI code&rdquo;. Platforms help: repository instructions (AGENTS.md), MCP servers for internal tools, sandboxes, policies and fast CI so agent-produced changes are verified quickly. Running a DevEx programme# DevEx improvement loop flowchart LR S[&#34;Survey + system data&lt;br/&gt;quarterly&#34;] --&gt; F[&#34;Find top friction&lt;br/&gt;by team and journey&#34;] F --&gt; P[&#34;Prioritise with teams&lt;br/&gt;platform roadmap&#34;] P --&gt; I[&#34;Improve&lt;br/&gt;golden paths, CI, docs, env&#34;] I --&gt; M[&#34;Measure change&#34;] M --&gt; S Baseline with a short survey and a few system metrics. Pick the top two or three friction points (for example &ldquo;CI takes 40 minutes&rdquo;, &ldquo;new environments take two weeks&rdquo;). Fix them as platform product work; communicate results. Re-measure every quarter. Quick check# What are the three core dimensions of DevEx? Feedback loops, cognitive load and flow state. What is the difference between the inner and outer loop? The inner loop is edit–build–test on a developer&rsquo;s machine; the outer loop is PR, CI, review, deploy and observe. Why combine surveys with system metrics? System metrics show where time goes; surveys reveal friction and satisfaction that systems cannot see; together they guide improvements. Why not measure individual productivity by commits? It is easily gamed, ignores collaboration and quality, and erodes trust; measure teams and systems instead. Give two platform-specific DevEx metrics. Time to first deploy for a new service; golden-path adoption rate (others: onboarding time, self-service rate, platform satisfaction). Summary# DevEx = feedback loops, cognitive load and flow state. Improve both inner and outer loops. Measure with DORA, SPACE, DevEx, DX Core 4 — surveys plus system data, at team level. Run a quarterly loop: measure, prioritise friction, improve, re-measure. References# Noda, Storey, Forsgren, Greiler, DevEx: What Actually Drives Productivity, ACM Queue, 2023. Forsgren et al., The SPACE of Developer Productivity, ACM Queue, 2021. DORA research. DX, DX Core 4.
d: What developer experience (DevEx) is, the three core dimensions (feedback loops, cognitive load, flow state), measurement frameworks (DORA, SPACE, DevEx, DX Core 4), surveys plus system metrics, platform metrics, inner loop vs outer loop, AI coding assistants, and how to run a DevEx improvement programme.

b: Simple definition# Kubernetes networking answers four questions: how Pods talk to each other, how clients find a stable address for a changing set of Pods (Services), how external traffic gets in (Gateway API / Ingress), and how traffic is restricted (NetworkPolicy). The network model — three rules# Every Pod gets its own IP address. Pods can reach all other Pods without NAT, on any node. Agents on a node can reach all Pods on that node. A CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin implements these rules — for example Cilium (eBPF), Calico, cloud-native CNIs such as the AWS VPC CNI and Azure CNI, or OVN-Kubernetes on OpenShift. Pod-to-Pod across nodes flowchart LR subgraph N1[&#34;Node 1&#34;] P1[&#34;Pod A&lt;br/&gt;10.0.1.5&#34;] --- V1[&#34;veth&#34;] --- B1[&#34;CNI data plane&#34;] end subgraph N2[&#34;Node 2&#34;] B2[&#34;CNI data plane&#34;] --- V2[&#34;veth&#34;] --- P2[&#34;Pod B&lt;br/&gt;10.0.2.7&#34;] end B1 &lt;--&gt;|&#34;routed or overlay&lt;br/&gt;(VXLAN / Geneve)&#34;| B2 Services: stable addresses for changing Pods# Pods come and go; their IPs change. A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances to the ready Pods that match its label selector (tracked in EndpointSlices). Type Reachable from Use ClusterIP (default) Inside the cluster Service-to-service calls NodePort Each node&rsquo;s IP on a high port Rarely directly; building block for LBs LoadBalancer Outside, via a cloud load balancer Exposing gateways or TCP services Headless (clusterIP: None) DNS returns Pod IPs StatefulSets, client-side load balancing ExternalName DNS alias Point to an external service How Service routing is implemented: kube-proxy programs iptables or nftables rules on every node (IPVS mode is deprecated as of 1.35), or an eBPF data plane (Cilium) replaces kube-proxy for better performance and observability. DNS: CoreDNS resolves orders.shop.svc.cluster.local to the Service IP. Within a namespace, orders is enough. Getting traffic in: Ingress → Gateway API# Ingress was the original API for HTTP routing, but it is limited (one resource for everything, routing details hidden in vendor annotations). The Gateway API is its successor: role-oriented, expressive and portable. Gateway API resources and roles flowchart TB GC[&#34;GatewayClass&lt;br/&gt;which implementation&lt;br/&gt;owner: infrastructure provider&#34;] --&gt; GW[&#34;Gateway&lt;br/&gt;listeners, ports, TLS&lt;br/&gt;owner: platform team&#34;] GW --&gt; R1[&#34;HTTPRoute&lt;br/&gt;/orders → orders Service&lt;br/&gt;owner: app team&#34;] GW --&gt; R2[&#34;GRPCRoute / TLSRoute / TCPRoute&#34;] R1 --&gt; S1[&#34;Service: orders&#34;] GatewayClass — the implementation (Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, NGINX Gateway Fabric, Kong, HAProxy, cloud gateways). Gateway — listeners, hostnames, certificates; owned by the platform team. HTTPRoute / GRPCRoute — path, header and weight-based routing (canaries), owned by app teams; ReferenceGrant controls cross-namespace references. Version noteingress-nginx retired The community ingress-nginx controller was retired in March 2026 (no further releases or security fixes). The Ingress API still works with other controllers, but new designs should use the Gateway API, and existing ingress-nginx users should migrate — its nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/* annotations do not carry over to other controllers. A request traced end to end# A request through Kubernetes networking · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ DNS (often managed by external-dns) resolves the hostname to the cloud load balancer. The load balancer forwards to the gateway&rsquo;s Pods. The Gateway terminates TLS; the matching HTTPRoute selects the backend Service. The Service (kube-proxy or eBPF) picks a ready endpoint Pod. The response returns along the same path. Network policies: default-deny# By default every Pod can talk to every Pod. NetworkPolicy restricts traffic by labels, namespaces and ports (enforced by the CNI). # 1. Deny all ingress in the namespace apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: { name: default-deny-ingress, namespace: shop } spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: [Ingress] --- # 2. Allow only the gateway to reach the orders Pods on 8080 apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: { name: allow-gateway-to-orders, namespace: shop } spec: podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders } } ingress: - from: - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: gateway } } ports: [{ port: 8080, protocol: TCP }] Start with default deny, then allow known flows (including DNS egress to CoreDNS). Advanced CNIs add L7 rules, FQDN-based egress, cluster-wide policies and the upcoming AdminNetworkPolicy for platform teams. Multi-cluster and egress# Egress control: egress gateways or FQDN policies so workloads reach only approved external hosts. Multi-cluster networking: Cilium Cluster Mesh, Submariner, service mesh multi-cluster, or global load balancing at the edge. IP planning: size Pod and Service CIDRs for growth; avoid overlaps with on-premises networks; consider IPv6/dual-stack. Common mistakes# Common mistakeOne LoadBalancer Service per app Costly and unmanageable. Expose a shared Gateway and route with HTTPRoutes. Common mistakeNo NetworkPolicies A compromised Pod can reach every database in the cluster. Default-deny per namespace. Common mistakeStaying on ingress-nginx It no longer receives security fixes. Plan the migration to Gateway API or a maintained controller. Quick check# What are the three rules of the Kubernetes network model? Every Pod has its own IP; Pods reach each other without NAT across nodes; node agents reach local Pods. Why do we need Services? Pod IPs change; a Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances to ready Pods selected by labels. What problem does the Gateway API solve over Ingress? b: Simple definition# Red Hat OpenShift is an enterprise Kubernetes platform: certified Kubernetes plus an integrated, supported set of components — operating system, networking, ingress, registry, monitoring, logging, security, CI/CD, GitOps, service mesh, virtualization and a developer portal — installed and upgraded as one product. OpenShift vs upstream Kubernetes# OpenShift = Kubernetes &#43; integrated platform flowchart TB subgraph OCP[&#34;OpenShift Container Platform&#34;] DEV[&#34;Developer experience&lt;br/&gt;console, Developer Hub (Backstage), odo, S2I&#34;] APP[&#34;Application services&lt;br/&gt;Pipelines (Tekton), GitOps (Argo CD), Service Mesh, Serverless&#34;] PLAT[&#34;Platform services&lt;br/&gt;Routes/Ingress, registry, monitoring, logging, OVN networking, OLM&#34;] K8S[&#34;Certified Kubernetes + CRI-O&#34;] OS[&#34;Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS&lt;br/&gt;immutable, managed by the cluster&#34;] DEV --&gt; APP --&gt; PLAT --&gt; K8S --&gt; OS end Area Upstream Kubernetes OpenShift Node OS Your choice RHCOS, managed via Machine Config Operator Runtime containerd/CRI-O CRI-O Ingress Choose a controller Routes (HAProxy router) + Ingress + Gateway API support Security defaults Pod Security Admission Security Context Constraints (SCCs) + PSA; containers run as random non-root UIDs Extensions Install operators yourself OperatorHub + Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) Builds External CI BuildConfigs, Source-to-Image (S2I), Shipwright CI/CD Choose tools OpenShift Pipelines (Tekton), OpenShift GitOps (Argo CD) Upgrades Component by component Over-the-air cluster upgrades via the Cluster Version Operator Support Community/vendor mix Single vendor for the whole stack Key OpenShift concepts# Projects — namespaces with extra annotations and default RBAC for teams. Routes — OpenShift&rsquo;s original way to expose HTTP(S) services with edge, passthrough or re-encrypt TLS. SCCs — cluster-level policies controlling privileges; the default restricted-v2 blocks root and privilege escalation. Many public images that assume root need small changes to run. Operators everywhere — the platform itself is managed by operators, so it self-heals and upgrades consistently. Machine API / MachineSets — declarative node provisioning and autoscaling on supported infrastructure. Developer and delivery features# Typical OpenShift delivery flow flowchart LR G[&#34;Git push&#34;] --&gt; P[&#34;OpenShift Pipelines&lt;br/&gt;Tekton: build, test, scan&#34;] P --&gt; R[(&#34;Internal / Quay registry&#34;)] P --&gt; C[&#34;Update config repo&#34;] C --&gt; A[&#34;OpenShift GitOps&lt;br/&gt;Argo CD&#34;] A --&gt; D[&#34;Deploy to projects&lt;br/&gt;across clusters&#34;] R --&gt; D OpenShift Pipelines — Tekton-based, Kubernetes-native pipelines (Tasks and Pipelines as CRDs), plus Pipelines-as-Code. OpenShift GitOps — supported Argo CD; recent releases add an Argo CD agent model for pull-based multi-cluster delivery. Red Hat Developer Hub — a supported Backstage distribution for an internal developer portal. OpenShift Service Mesh (Istio-based) and Serverless (Knative). OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt) runs VMs next to containers — a common path for migrating VMware estates; 4.21 added live cross-cluster VM migration. OpenShift AI for model serving and MLOps; recent releases support Dynamic Resource Allocation for GPUs. Deployment options# Option Notes OpenShift Container Platform Self-managed on bare metal, VMware, OpenStack or cloud ROSA (Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS), ARO (Azure Red Hat OpenShift), OpenShift Dedicated Managed by Red Hat and the cloud provider Single-node / compact clusters Edge and small sites Advanced Cluster Management (ACM) Multi-cluster governance, placement and policy Advanced Cluster Security (ACS) Image scanning, runtime detection, compliance (StackRox) When to choose OpenShift# Good fit: regulated enterprises wanting one supported platform; hybrid or on-premises estates; VMware migrations; teams that value integrated security defaults and over-the-air upgrades. Consider alternatives when: you are cloud-only and comfortable assembling managed Kubernetes with your chosen add-ons, or licence cost outweighs the integration value. Common mistakes# Common mistakeRunning images that require root They fail under the restricted SCC. Build images that run as arbitrary non-root users (group 0 writable directories) rather than loosening SCCs. Common mistakeUsing OpenShift like plain Kubernetes and ignoring its operators Hand-installing alternatives to platform components increases upgrade friction. Use the supported operators unless there is a clear reason. Quick check# What does OpenShift add to Kubernetes? An integrated, supported stack: RHCOS, CRI-O, OVN networking, Routes, registry, monitoring, logging, SCC security, OperatorHub/OLM, Pipelines, GitOps, Service Mesh, Virtualization, Developer Hub and managed over-the-air upgrades. What is an SCC? A Security Context Constraint — OpenShift&rsquo;s policy controlling what privileges Pods may use; the default restricted profile runs containers as random non-root UIDs. What are OpenShift Pipelines and GitOps based on? Tekton and Argo CD respectively. What is ROSA? Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS — managed OpenShift jointly operated by Red Hat and AWS. Why do teams run VMs on OpenShift? OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt) lets them run and migrate VMs alongside containers on one platform, for example when moving off VMware. Summary# OpenShift is Kubernetes plus a supported, integrated platform managed by operators. Key differences: RHCOS, SCCs, Routes, OLM, built-in CI/CD (Tekton) and GitOps (Argo CD). Available self-managed or as ROSA/ARO; ACM and ACS for fleets and security. Strong fit for regulated, hybrid and VM-migration scenarios. References# Red Hat, OpenShift Container Platform 4.21 release notes. Red Hat blog, Red Hat OpenShift 4.21. Red Hat blog, What&rsquo;s new in OpenShift Virtualization 4.21.
d: What OpenShift adds to Kubernetes: integrated platform components, Routes, Security Context Constraints, Operators and OperatorHub, builds and S2I, OpenShift Pipelines (Tekton), OpenShift GitOps (Argo CD), Service Mesh, Virtualization, Developer Hub, deployment options (ROSA, ARO, on-premises) and how it compares with upstream Kubernetes.
