b: Simple definition# Resilience is a system&rsquo;s ability to keep serving users — perhaps in a degraded way — when parts fail, and to recover quickly. Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan and capability to restore service and data after a large failure such as losing a region. Think in failure domains# Failure domains, small to large flowchart LR P[&#34;Process / container&#34;] --&gt; PD[&#34;Pod&#34;] --&gt; N[&#34;Node&#34;] --&gt; Z[&#34;Availability zone&#34;] --&gt; R[&#34;Region&#34;] --&gt; CP[&#34;Cloud provider&#34;] D[&#34;Dependencies: DB, queue,&lt;br/&gt;third-party API, DNS, IdP&#34;] -.-&gt; PD For each domain ask: what fails, how do we detect it, what is the blast radius, how do we recover, and how long does it take? Resilience patterns# Pattern What it does Where Redundancy Multiple replicas across nodes and zones Deployments, topology spread, multi-AZ databases Timeouts Never wait forever Every network call; shorter than the caller&rsquo;s timeout Retries with backoff + jitter Survive transient errors Idempotent operations only; with a retry budget Circuit breaker Stop calling a failing dependency; fail fast Client libraries (Resilience4j) or mesh Bulkhead Isolate resources so one failure cannot exhaust all Separate pools, queues, node pools Load shedding / rate limiting Reject excess work early to protect the core Gateways, services Graceful degradation Serve a reduced experience Cached data, default recommendations, read-only mode Idempotency Safe to repeat requests Idempotency keys on writes Queue-based load levelling Absorb bursts asynchronously Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ Resilient call to a dependency flowchart LR C[&#34;Caller&#34;] --&gt; T[&#34;Timeout&#34;] T --&gt; R[&#34;Retry: backoff + jitter,&lt;br/&gt;budget&#34;] R --&gt; CB{&#34;Circuit&lt;br/&gt;breaker&#34;} CB --&gt;|&#34;closed&#34;| D[&#34;Dependency&#34;] CB --&gt;|&#34;open&#34;| F[&#34;Fallback&lt;br/&gt;cache / default / degrade&#34;] D --&gt;|&#34;errors exceed threshold&#34;| CB Common mistakeRetry storms Retries at the client, mesh and gateway multiply traffic onto an already failing service. Retry in one layer, with budgets, backoff and jitter. Kubernetes resilience features# Multiple replicas + topology spread constraints across zones. PodDisruptionBudgets protect availability during drains and upgrades. Readiness probes keep unready Pods out of rotation; graceful shutdown with preStop and termination grace periods. Priority classes keep critical workloads scheduled under pressure. Autoscaling headroom; node pools spread across zones. RPO and RTO# Term Question Driven by RPO — Recovery Point Objective How much data can we lose? Backup frequency, replication mode RTO — Recovery Time Objective How long can we be down? DR strategy, automation, rehearsal DR strategies# DR strategies: cost vs recovery speed flowchart LR BR[&#34;Backup &amp; restore&lt;br/&gt;RTO hours–days&lt;br/&gt;lowest cost&#34;] --&gt; PL[&#34;Pilot light&lt;br/&gt;core data replicated,&lt;br/&gt;compute off&#34;] PL --&gt; WS[&#34;Warm standby&lt;br/&gt;scaled-down copy running&lt;br/&gt;RTO minutes&#34;] WS --&gt; AA[&#34;Active-active&lt;br/&gt;multi-region serving&lt;br/&gt;RTO ~0, highest cost&#34;] Strategy RPO RTO Cost Notes Backup &amp; restore Hours Hours–days Low Restore clusters from Git + backups Pilot light Minutes Hours Medium-low Data replicated; infra created on failover Warm standby Seconds–minutes Minutes Medium Smaller running copy, scale up on failover Active-active ~0–seconds ~0 High Data consistency across regions is the hard part Kubernetes helps: clusters and apps are rebuildable from Git (GitOps), making backup-restore and pilot light much faster than for hand-built estates. Backups# Velero: backs up Kubernetes objects and persistent volumes (snapshots or file-level), schedules, restores to another cluster. Database-native backups and point-in-time recovery (managed services or operators such as CloudNativePG). Registry replication across regions; secrets store replication. Test restores regularly — an untested backup is a hope, not a plan. Chaos engineering# Deliberately inject failures in a controlled way to find weaknesses before they cause incidents. Chaos experiment loop flowchart LR H[&#34;Hypothesis&lt;br/&gt;&#39;losing one zone keeps&lt;br/&gt;checkout SLO&#39;&#34;] --&gt; E[&#34;Experiment&lt;br/&gt;small blast radius,&lt;br/&gt;abort conditions&#34;] E --&gt; O[&#34;Observe SLIs&#34;] O --&gt; L[&#34;Learn + fix&#34;] L --&gt; H Tools: LitmusChaos, Chaos Mesh (CNCF), AWS Fault Injection Service, Azure Chaos Studio, Gremlin. Start in non-production with game days; progress to production with tight safeguards. Typical experiments: kill Pods, drain a node, block a zone, add latency to a dependency, fail DNS, expire certificates. Common mistakes# Common mistakeDR plans never rehearsed The first real failover is when you discover missing permissions, stale runbooks and hidden dependencies. Rehearse at least twice a year. Common mistakeMulti-region for every service Active-active is expensive and complex. Match the DR strategy to each service&rsquo;s business RTO/RPO. Quick check# What is the difference between RPO and RTO? RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss (time); RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime. Name four resilience patterns. Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads (also load shedding, graceful degradation, idempotency). What is a PodDisruptionBudget for? It limits how many Pods of an application can be voluntarily disrupted at once, protecting availability during drains and upgrades. Compare warm standby and active-active. Warm standby runs a scaled-down copy that takes over in minutes; active-active serves from multiple regions continuously with near-zero RTO but higher cost and data-consistency complexity. What is chaos engineering? Running controlled experiments that inject failures to test hypotheses about resilience and fix weaknesses before real
d: Designing cloud native systems to survive failure: failure domains, redundancy across zones and regions, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding, graceful degradation, Kubernetes resilience features, RPO and RTO, DR strategies from backup-restore to active-active, backup with Velero, and chaos engineering.

b: The design brief# &ldquo;A bank with 300 delivery teams (about 2,500 developers) runs a mix of VMs and early Kubernetes clusters. New services take six weeks to reach production through tickets. Design an internal developer platform that gets a new service to production in under a day — securely and compliantly.&rdquo; 1. Requirements# Functional Self-service creation of services (Java, Node, Python), databases, queues and environments. Standard CI/CD with security scanning, signing and progressive delivery. Catalog of all services with owners, docs, dependencies, runtime status and cost. Environments: dev, test, staging, prod; ephemeral preview environments per PR. Non-functional Requirement Target New service to production &lt; 1 day (target: first deploy to dev in &lt; 15 minutes) Platform availability 99.9% for CI, registry, GitOps; 99.95% for production clusters Compliance Segregation of duties, audit trail, change evidence, encryption, EU data residency Scale ~3,000 services, ~25,000 Pods in production, ~150 deployments/day Security Signed images only; least privilege; no cluster credentials in CI 2. Sizing (rough)# 3,000 services × average 3 replicas × 0.5 vCPU / 1 GiB → ~4,500 vCPU / 9 TiB requested in prod; plus non-prod ≈ 1.5× → plan for ~12,000 vCPU across environments with autoscaling. Clusters: prod per region (2 regions) split by tenancy class (general, regulated) → 4 prod clusters; non-prod 4–6 clusters; platform/management cluster(s). CI: ~5,000 builds/day peak → autoscaled runners on Kubernetes. 3. Architecture# Internal developer platform reference architecture · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Audit: Git history + Argo CD events + API audit logs + automated change records = evidence. 7. Reliability of the platform itself# Platform components have SLOs and on-call; HA across zones; GitOps for platform config. Break-glass access procedure, audited. b: Simple definition# FinOps is an operational framework and cultural practice that maximises the business value of cloud (and now technology) spending through collaboration between engineering, finance and business — making cost visible, owned and optimised continuously. The FinOps Framework# FinOps lifecycle phases flowchart LR I[&#34;Inform&lt;br/&gt;visibility, allocation,&lt;br/&gt;showback, forecasting&#34;] --&gt; O[&#34;Optimize&lt;br/&gt;rightsizing, rates,&lt;br/&gt;architecture&#34;] O --&gt; OP[&#34;Operate&lt;br/&gt;policies, budgets,&lt;br/&gt;continuous improvement&#34;] OP --&gt; I Principles (FinOps Foundation): teams collaborate; business value drives decisions; everyone takes ownership of their usage; data is accessible, timely and accurate; FinOps is enabled centrally; take advantage of the variable cost model of the cloud. Scopes extend FinOps beyond public cloud — SaaS, data centres, licensing and AI — and the 2026 framework adds explicit guidance on aligning with executive strategy. FinOps for AI (model API tokens, GPUs, AI platforms) is now a major focus area. FOCUS: one billing format# The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) standardises billing data columns (cost, usage, service, region, tags, commitments) across cloud and SaaS providers, so cost tools and dashboards work across vendors. Major clouds publish FOCUS-format exports; check the current spec version before building on it. Kubernetes cost: the allocation problem# Cloud bills show nodes; teams own Pods. Kubernetes cost tools split node cost by what workloads request (and use). From cloud bill to team showback flowchart LR BILL[&#34;Cloud bill&lt;br/&gt;nodes, disks, LBs, egress&#34;] --&gt; OC[&#34;OpenCost / Kubecost&lt;br/&gt;price × requests vs usage&#34;] K8S[&#34;Kubernetes metadata&lt;br/&gt;namespace, labels, owner&#34;] --&gt; OC OC --&gt; NS[&#34;Cost per namespace,&lt;br/&gt;team, app, environment&#34;] OC --&gt; IDLE[&#34;Idle / unallocated cost&#34;] NS --&gt; PORTAL[&#34;Showback in portal&lt;br/&gt;+ budgets, alerts&#34;] OpenCost (CNCF incubating) is the open standard and engine; Kubecost and cloud tools build on similar models. Require labels/annotations for team, app, environment and cost centre (enforced by admission policy). Report idle cost (requested but unused, and unallocated node capacity) explicitly. Show cost in the developer portal next to each service. Optimisation levers# Lever What to do Typical saving Rightsize requests Use VPA recommendations / usage percentiles; in-place resize Large — requests are often 2–5× actual use Autoscale Pods HPA/KEDA; scale to zero for idle non-prod Medium Bin-pack nodes Karpenter consolidation, fewer larger nodes, right instance families Medium–large Spot / preemptible For stateless, fault-tolerant and batch workloads Up to ~60–90% on those nodes Commitments Savings plans, reserved instances, committed use for the steady baseline 20–60% on committed portion Schedule non-prod Shut down dev/test outside working hours ~65% of non-prod compute Architecture ARM (Graviton/Ampere/Cobalt), managed services, data transfer design, storage tiers Varies Observability cost Cardinality, sampling, retention Often significant Unit economics# Total cost alone says little. Track cost per business unit: cost per order, per active customer, per API call, per tenant. Unit cost falling while total cost rises is often healthy growth. FinOps for AI# Track cost per inference / per token / per task, GPU utilisation and idle GPU time. Use AI gateways for per-team quotas and showback; route to cheaper models; cache prompts. Schedule GPUs efficiently (DRA, sharing/partitioning, queueing with Kueue); use spot for training where possible. GreenOps# Carbon and cost usually move together: rightsizing, scaling to zero, efficient instance types and choosing lower-carbon regions reduce both. Cloud carbon dashboards and tools like Kepler (Kubernetes energy metrics) make it visible. Platform guardrails for cost# Required cost labels at admission; default requests via LimitRange; namespace ResourceQuotas. Budgets and anomaly alerts per team; cost shown in Backstage. Non-prod schedules and TTLs for preview environments. Golden-path defaults with sensible sizes and autoscaling. Common mistakes# Common mistakeFinOps as a finance-only report Engineers make most cost decisions. Put cost data in their tools and give them ownership. Common mistakeInflated requests &ldquo;just in case&rdquo; Requests drive both scheduling and cost. Rightsize with data; rely on autoscaling for peaks. Common mistakeCommitments before optimisation Committing to an over-provisioned baseline locks in waste. Rightsize first, then commit. Quick check# What are the three FinOps phases? Inform, Optimize and Operate — a continuous loop. What is FOCUS? The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification — a common format for billing data across cloud and SaaS providers. Why is Kubernetes cost allocation hard and how is it done? Bills show nodes while teams own Pods; tools like OpenCost split node and shared costs by requests and usage using namespaces and labels. Name three Kubernetes cost-optimisation levers. Rightsizing requests, autoscaling and bin-packing nodes (Karpenter), spot instances, commitments, and scheduling non-prod off. What is unit economics in FinOps? Measuring cost per unit of business value, such as cost per order or per customer, to judge efficiency as the business grows. Summary# FinOps makes cost visible, owned and optimised through engineering–finance collaboration. Inform → Optimize → Operate; scopes now include SaaS, data centres and AI. Allocate Kubernetes cost with OpenCost and enforced labels; show cost in developer tools. Rightsize, autoscale, bin-pack, use spot and commitments; track unit economics; consider carbon. References# FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework and 2026 framework update. FOCUS specification. OpenCost. FinOps Foundation, FinOps for AI.
d: Managing cloud and Kubernetes cost as an engineering discipline: the FinOps Framework (principles, phases, domains, scopes), the FOCUS billing standard, Kubernetes cost allocation with OpenCost, rightsizing, autoscaling and bin-packing, spot and commitments, unit economics, FinOps for AI, GreenOps, and platform guardrails.

b: Simple definition# Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a versioned package of templated Kubernetes manifests; values customise it per environment; installing a chart creates a release that Helm can upgrade and roll back. How Helm works# Chart &#43; values → manifests → release flowchart LR C[&#34;Chart&lt;br/&gt;templates/*.yaml&lt;br/&gt;Chart.yaml, values.yaml&#34;] --&gt; R[&#34;helm template / install&lt;br/&gt;render with Go templates&#34;] V[&#34;values-prod.yaml&lt;br/&gt;--set image.tag=1.4.2&#34;] --&gt; R R --&gt; M[&#34;Kubernetes manifests&#34;] M --&gt; K[&#34;Cluster&#34;] K --&gt; REL[(&#34;Release record&lt;br/&gt;revision 1, 2, 3…&lt;br/&gt;stored as Secret&#34;)] Chart structure# orders/ ├── Chart.yaml # name, version (chart), appVersion (app), dependencies ├── values.yaml # defaults ├── values.schema.json # validates values ├── templates/ │ ├── deployment.yaml │ ├── service.yaml │ ├── httproute.yaml │ ├── hpa.yaml │ ├── _helpers.tpl # named templates (labels, names) │ └── NOTES.txt └── charts/ # sub-chart dependencies A template fragment: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: {{ include &#34;orders.fullname&#34; . }} labels: {{- include &#34;orders.labels&#34; . | nindent 4 }} spec: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} template: spec: containers: - name: orders image: &#34;{{ .Values.image.repository }}@{{ .Values.image.digest }}&#34; resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} Everyday commands# Task Command Install / upgrade helm upgrade --install orders oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts/orders --version 1.4.2 -f values-prod.yaml -n shop Preview helm template … or helm diff upgrade … (plugin) History / rollback helm history orders -n shop, helm rollback orders 3 -n shop Lint / test helm lint, helm test orders Package / publish helm package ., helm push orders-1.4.2.tgz oci://ghcr.io/acme/charts Helm 4# Helm 4 (November 2025, Helm&rsquo;s 10th anniversary) modernised the tool: Server-side apply by default for new releases — better field ownership and conflict detection, aligned with GitOps tools. Releases created by Helm 3 keep client-side apply until changed. WebAssembly plugins — an optional sandboxed plugin runtime; post-renderers become plugins. Install by digest from OCI registries for supply-chain integrity. kstatus-based waiting for resource readiness. Flag changes: --atomic → --rollback-on-failure, --force → --force-replace. Helm 3 charts (apiVersion v2) continue to work. Best practices# Version charts with SemVer; separate chart version from appVersion. Values schema (values.schema.json) to catch bad values early. Sensible, secure defaults: resources, probes, non-root security context, PodDisruptionBudget. Keep templates simple — heavy logic makes charts unreadable; prefer a few well-named values. Standard labels (app.kubernetes.io/name, instance, version, part-of). No secrets in values files — reference External Secrets. Publish to OCI registries; sign charts (cosign) and verify. Test: helm lint, unit tests (helm-unittest), schema validation (kubeconform), policy checks (Kyverno CLI / Conftest), and install tests in kind/k3d in CI. Library charts for shared templates across many services (a common platform-team pattern). Composition# Approach Use Umbrella chart One chart with dependencies for a whole system Helmfile Declarative list of releases and values per environment GitOps (Argo CD / Flux) Git holds chart versions + values; the controller renders and applies — the recommended production approach Helm with GitOps# Helm rendered by Argo CD flowchart LR REG[(&#34;OCI registry&lt;br/&gt;orders chart 1.4.2&#34;)] --&gt; AR[&#34;Argo CD Application&lt;br/&gt;chart + version + values&#34;] GIT[(&#34;Config repo&lt;br/&gt;values-prod.yaml&#34;)] --&gt; AR AR --&gt;|&#34;render + sync&#34;| K[&#34;Cluster&#34;] Argo CD renders the chart and applies manifests (it does not create Helm release records); Flux&rsquo;s Helm controller performs real Helm releases. Either way, Git records which chart version and values run where. Common mistakes# Common mistakeRunning helm upgrade by hand in production Changes are not reviewed or recorded in Git and drift between environments. Let GitOps apply charts. Common mistakeCharts as programming languages Deeply nested conditionals and loops make charts impossible to review. Keep charts boring; split them if needed. Quick check# What is the difference between a chart, values and a release? A chart is the package of templates; values customise it; a release is an installed instance of a chart with its revision history. What changed in Helm 4? Server-side apply by default for new releases, WebAssembly-based plugins, install by digest from OCI registries, kstatus waiting and renamed flags such as --rollback-on-failure. Kustomize or Helm? Helm for distributable, versioned packages and third-party software; Kustomize for overlays of your own manifests — both work with GitOps. How do you test a chart? Lint, unit-test templates, validate rendered manifests against schemas and policies, and install it in a throwaway cluster in CI. Summary# Helm packages templated manifests into versioned charts; values customise; releases track revisions. Helm 4 brings server-side apply, Wasm plugins and digest-based installs. Keep charts simple, secure by default, schema-validated, tested and published to OCI. Apply charts in production through GitOps. References# Helm documentation and Helm 4 overview. Chart best practices. Jimmy Song, Helm v4: paradigm convergence and plugin system rebuild.
d: Helm explained simply: charts, templates, values and releases; chart structure; install, upgrade and rollback; OCI registries; Helm 4 changes (server-side apply, WebAssembly plugins, install by digest); chart best practices, testing, security, umbrella charts, Helmfile, and Helm with GitOps.

b: Simple definition# A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication for you: encrypts it with mutual TLS, applies traffic rules (retries, timeouts, canary weights), enforces identity-based authorisation, and emits telemetry — without changing application code. What a mesh gives you# Capability Example Zero-trust security Automatic mTLS between all workloads; policies like &ldquo;only checkout may call payments&rdquo; based on workload identity (SPIFFE IDs) Traffic management Weighted routing for canaries, header-based routing, mirroring, fault injection Resilience Timeouts, retries with budgets, circuit breaking, outlier detection Observability Golden metrics (requests, errors, latency) and traces for every hop Architectures: sidecar vs sidecarless# Sidecar mesh vs ambient (sidecarless) mesh flowchart TB subgraph Sidecar[&#34;Sidecar mode&#34;] A1[&#34;App&#34;] --- P1[&#34;Envoy sidecar&#34;] P1 &lt;--&gt;|&#34;mTLS + L7&#34;| P2[&#34;Envoy sidecar&#34;] P2 --- A2[&#34;App&#34;] end subgraph Ambient[&#34;Ambient mode (Istio)&#34;] B1[&#34;App&#34;] --&gt; Z1[&#34;ztunnel&lt;br/&gt;per node, L4 mTLS&#34;] Z1 &lt;--&gt;|&#34;HBONE mTLS&#34;| Z2[&#34;ztunnel&#34;] Z1 -.-&gt;|&#34;only if L7 needed&#34;| W[&#34;Waypoint proxy&lt;br/&gt;per namespace/service, L7&#34;] W -.-&gt; Z2 Z2 --&gt; B2[&#34;App&#34;] end Sidecar — an Envoy proxy in every Pod. Full L7 features everywhere, but extra CPU/memory per Pod and restarts to upgrade proxies. Istio ambient mode (GA since Istio 1.24, late 2024) — a per-node ztunnel provides L4 mTLS and identity for all Pods; optional waypoint proxies add L7 features only where needed. Far less overhead and no app restarts to join the mesh. eBPF meshes (Cilium) — use the CNI&rsquo;s eBPF data plane for L3/L4 and a shared per-node Envoy for L7. Choosing a mesh# Istio Linkerd Cilium Service Mesh Model Sidecar or ambient Lightweight Rust sidecar eBPF + per-node Envoy Strengths Most features; multi-cluster; Gateway API; ambient reduces cost Simplicity, low overhead, strong defaults One stack for CNI, policy, mesh, observability (Hubble) Watch out Complexity; learn its APIs Fewer advanced traffic features Ties mesh to the CNI choice OpenShift Service Mesh is based on Istio. Do you need a mesh?# Mesh decision flowchart TD A{&#34;Regulatory or zero-trust need&lt;br/&gt;for mTLS everywhere?&#34;} --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| M[&#34;Mesh (ambient for low overhead)&#34;] A --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| B{&#34;Many services, polyglot,&lt;br/&gt;need uniform traffic control?&#34;} B --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| M B --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| C[&#34;No mesh yet: Gateway API,&lt;br/&gt;NetworkPolicy, library resilience,&lt;br/&gt;OpenTelemetry&#34;] Common mistakes# Common mistakeRetries at every layer Client library, mesh and gateway all retrying multiplies load during an outage (retry storms). Retry in one place with budgets and timeouts. Common mistakeAdopting a mesh for one feature If you only need ingress routing or metrics, a mesh adds more operational load than value. Quick check# What does a service mesh provide? mTLS and workload identity, traffic management, resilience features and telemetry for service-to-service traffic without code changes. What are ztunnel and waypoint proxies in Istio ambient mode? ztunnel is a per-node proxy providing L4 mTLS and identity; waypoints are optional proxies that add L7 features for selected namespaces or services. Why consider ambient over sidecars? Lower resource overhead, no per-Pod proxies, no application restarts to join or upgrade, and L7 cost only where needed. When might you not need a mesh? Few services, no zero-trust mTLS requirement, and needs met by Gateway API, NetworkPolicies, libraries and OpenTelemetry. Summary# A mesh adds mTLS, traffic control, resilience and telemetry transparently. Sidecarless (Istio ambient, Cilium) is now mainstream and cheaper to run. Choose by need: Istio for features, Linkerd for simplicity, Cilium for a unified eBPF stack — or no mesh. References# Istio, Ambient mode overview. Linkerd, Cilium Service Mesh. SPIFFE.
d: What a service mesh adds — mTLS, traffic management, resilience and telemetry — sidecar vs sidecarless (Istio ambient with ztunnel and waypoints, Cilium), how to choose Istio, Linkerd or Cilium, and when you do not need a mesh.
t: Service Mesh: Istio, Linkerd, Cilium and Ambient Mode

b: The design brief# &ldquo;A digital bank&rsquo;s customer-facing services (login, accounts, payments) must stay available 24x7 even if an entire cloud region fails. Design the Kubernetes platform and the failover approach.&rdquo; 1. Requirements and SLOs# Service tier SLO (availability) RTO RPO Tier 0: login, balances, payments initiation 99.95% monthly ≤ 15 min regional failover ≤ 1 min (payments ledger: 0 for committed transactions) Tier 1: statements, notifications 99.9% ≤ 1 h ≤ 15 min Tier 2: analytics, back-office 99.5% ≤ 24 h ≤ 24 h Other requirements: EU data residency (two EU regions), PCI DSS scope isolation, peak 3,000 requests/s, deployments several times a day without downtime. 2. Topology# Multi-region Kubernetes platform · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Two regions, each with production clusters spread across three availability zones. Tier 0 runs active-active for stateless services with a single-writer ledger (see data below); Tier 1 warm standby; Tier 2 backup and restore. Separate PCI cluster per region for card-processing workloads. A GitOps hub (Argo CD with ApplicationSets, itself deployed in both regions) keeps both regions on the same reviewed configuration. 3. Traffic management and failover# Health-based regional failover sequenceDiagram participant U as Users participant G as Global DNS / GSLB participant A as Region A gateway participant B as Region B gateway participant O as On-call + runbook U-&gt;&gt;G: resolve api.bank.example G-&gt;&gt;A: health checks OK → route 50/50 (Tier 0) G-&gt;&gt;B: health checks OK Note over A: Region A degraded: SLO burn, health checks failing G-&gt;&gt;G: mark A unhealthy (automatic) G--&gt;&gt;U: answers point to region B only O-&gt;&gt;B: scale up (pre-approved), promote replicas for Tier 1 O-&gt;&gt;O: comms, status page, incident command Global DNS / anycast load balancing with health checks on synthetic transactions, not just TCP. Low DNS TTLs (30–60 s) and clients that honour them. Capacity: each region can carry 100% of Tier 0 peak (N+1 at region level) — the single most important cost decision. Automatic traffic failover for stateless tiers; human-approved promotion for data stores where split-brain risk exists. 4. Data# Data Approach Trade-off Payments ledger Single-writer primary in region A with synchronous replica in another zone and semi-sync/async cross-region replica; or a globally consistent database (for example Spanner-class or CockroachDB/YugabyteDB) Synchronous cross-region adds latency; async risks small data loss → business decides Customer profile Multi-region database with async replication; conflict-free updates via ownership by region Eventual consistency for reads Sessions / cache Regional Redis; sessions in signed tokens to survive failover Cache warm-up after failover Events Kafka per region with MirrorMaker 2 / cluster linking Duplicate handling via idempotent consumers Object storage Cross-region replication Replication lag 5. Delivery across regions# Same artifacts (by digest) and same Git state in both regions; ApplicationSets with region labels. Progressive rollout across regions: canary in region A → full region A → region B, with automated analysis (Argo Rollouts) and an error-budget gate. Infrastructure (clusters, networks, databases) as code (Terraform/OpenTofu or Crossplane), reproducible in a new region. 6. Observability# OpenTelemetry in all services; per-region Collector gateways; global query layer (Thanos/Mimir) so dashboards see both regions. SLOs per tier and region with multi-window burn-rate alerts. Synthetic probes from several external locations per critical journey. 7. Security# Separate cloud accounts/subscriptions per environment and PCI scope; private clusters; WAF and DDoS protection at the edge. mTLS (service mesh ambient mode) for Tier 0 services; default-deny NetworkPolicies. Signed images only; secrets in a replicated Vault/KMS per region; break-glass access audited. 8. DR runbooks and drills# Drill Frequency Success criterion Zone failure (drain all nodes in a zone) Monthly in staging, quarterly in prod SLO maintained Regional failover of Tier 0 Quarterly RTO ≤ 15 min, no data loss beyond RPO Restore Tier 2 from backup into a new cluster Twice a year Within RTO Dependency failure (IdP, DNS, payment network latency) Game days Graceful degradation works Automate failover steps in runbooks-as-code; record timings; feed gaps into the backlog. 9. Cost# Region-level N+1 roughly doubles Tier 0 compute — offset by spot for stateless non-critical services, rightsizing, Karpenter consolidation and commitments for the baseline. Warm standby for Tier 1 runs at ~25–30% capacity, scaling on failover. Cross-region data transfer is a material line item; design replication volume consciously. 10. Trade-offs# Decision Chosen Alternative Tier 0 compute Active-active Warm standby: cheaper, longer RTO Ledger Single writer + replicas Globally consistent DB: simpler failover, higher latency and cost Failover trigger Automatic for traffic, human for data promotion Fully automatic: faster, split-brain risk Cluster model Per region × tier, PCI separate Single large cluster per region: cheaper, larger blast radius TipWhat makes this design strong Tiered RTO/RPO agreed with the business, capacity for a full region loss, data consistency treated explicitly, identical Git-defined regions, and drills that prove the numbers. Quick check# Why must each region be able to carry 100% of Tier 0 load? Because after a regional failure the surviving region receives all traffic; without that headroom, failover becomes an outage. Why is data promotion often human-approved while traffic failover is automatic? Promoting a database replica during a partial failure risks split-brain and data loss; a brief human decision is safer, while stateless traffic can shift automatically. How do GitOps and IaC help DR? Regions and clusters are reproducible from code, so
d: A complete system design for a multi-region Kubernetes platform serving a 24x7 digital bank: requirements and SLOs, region and zone topology, traffic management and failover, data replication, GitOps across regions, observability, security, DR runbooks and drills, cost, and trade-offs.
t: System Design: A Highly Available Multi-Region Kubernetes Platform

b: Simple definition# Continuous integration (CI) — every change is merged often, built and tested automatically, producing a versioned artifact. Continuous delivery (CD) — every artifact that passes the pipeline can be released at any time with the push of a button. Continuous deployment — every passing change is released automatically. Progressive delivery — releases are exposed gradually (canary, feature flags) and rolled back automatically if metrics degrade. The pipeline# A cloud native CI/CD pipeline with gates flowchart LR C[&#34;Commit / PR&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Build + unit tests&#34;] B --&gt; S[&#34;Static analysis&lt;br/&gt;SAST, secrets, IaC scan&#34;] S --&gt; I[&#34;Build image&lt;br/&gt;SBOM + provenance&#34;] I --&gt; V[&#34;Image scan + sign&#34;] V --&gt; DT[&#34;Deploy to test&lt;br/&gt;via GitOps&#34;] DT --&gt; IT[&#34;Integration, contract,&lt;br/&gt;e2e, performance tests&#34;] IT --&gt; ST[&#34;Staging&lt;br/&gt;security DAST&#34;] ST --&gt; G{&#34;Gates: tests, policy,&lt;br/&gt;risk, approval&#34;} G --&gt; PR[&#34;Production&lt;br/&gt;canary&#34;] PR --&gt; M{&#34;Metrics healthy?&#34;} M --&gt;|&#34;yes&#34;| F[&#34;Full rollout&#34;] M --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| RB[&#34;Automatic rollback&#34;] Principles# Build once, promote the same artifact (by digest) through every environment; only configuration changes. Fast feedback: commit stage under 10 minutes; slower tests later and in parallel. Everything as code: pipelines, infrastructure, policies, environments. Shift security left but also verify at deploy time and runtime. Small batches: trunk-based development, short-lived branches, feature flags. CI pushes artifacts; CD pulls desired state — CI should not hold production cluster credentials (GitOps). CI tools# Tool Strengths Notes GitHub Actions Huge marketplace, close to code, OIDC to clouds Self-hosted runners on Kubernetes (Actions Runner Controller) GitLab CI Integrated DevSecOps platform, built-in scanners Strong for all-in-one setups Jenkins Extremely flexible, huge plugin ecosystem Operational burden; plugin sprawl Tekton Kubernetes-native CRDs (Tasks, Pipelines); OpenShift Pipelines Building block for platforms Azure DevOps, CircleCI, Buildkite Managed options — DevSecOps in the pipeline# Stage Checks Tools (examples) Code SAST, secrets detection, licence checks SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeQL, gitleaks Dependencies SCA / vulnerable libraries Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check IaC &amp; manifests Misconfigurations, policies Checkov, Trivy config, Kyverno CLI, Conftest Image CVEs, SBOM, provenance, signature Trivy, Grype, Syft, cosign, SLSA generators Running app DAST OWASP ZAP Runtime Behaviour detection Falco, cloud security tools Deployment strategies# Rolling, blue-green and canary flowchart TB subgraph Rolling[&#34;Rolling update&#34;] R1[&#34;v1 v1 v1&#34;] --&gt; R2[&#34;v2 v1 v1&#34;] --&gt; R3[&#34;v2 v2 v1&#34;] --&gt; R4[&#34;v2 v2 v2&#34;] end subgraph BG[&#34;Blue-green&#34;] B1[&#34;Blue v1 ← 100% traffic&#34;] --&gt; B2[&#34;Green v2 ready, tested&#34;] --&gt; B3[&#34;Switch: Green ← 100%&#34;] end subgraph CA[&#34;Canary&#34;] C1[&#34;v2 5%&#34;] --&gt; C2[&#34;analyse metrics&#34;] --&gt; C3[&#34;v2 25% → 50% → 100%&#34;] end Strategy Pros Cons Rolling (Deployment default) Simple, no extra capacity Mixed versions during rollout; slow rollback Blue-green Instant switch and rollback Double capacity; database changes must be compatible Canary Real-traffic validation with small blast radius Needs good metrics and traffic splitting Feature flags Decouple deploy from release; per-user targeting Flag debt; needs governance (OpenFeature standard) Shadow / mirroring Test with production traffic, no user impact Side effects must be handled Argo Rollouts and Flagger automate canary and blue-green on Kubernetes: shift traffic via Gateway API, mesh or ingress, run analysis against Prometheus/Datadog metrics (error rate, latency) and roll back automatically. apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: Rollout metadata: { name: orders } spec: strategy: canary: steps: - setWeight: 10 - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: success-rate }] } - setWeight: 50 - pause: { duration: 10m } - setWeight: 100 Database changes# Expand-and-contract migrations keep old and new versions compatible: add columns/tables first (expand), deploy code that uses both, migrate data, then remove old structures (contract) in a later release. Tools: Flyway, Liquibase. Measuring delivery: DORA metrics# Metric Elite performers (indicative) Deployment frequency On demand, many per day Lead time for changes Less than a day Change failure rate Low (single-digit to ~15%) Failed deployment recovery time Less than an hour DORA&rsquo;s research also tracks reliability and shows that speed and stability improve together with good practices. Common mistakes# Common mistakeRebuilding the image per environment You test one artifact and deploy another. Build once and promote by digest. Common mistakeManual gates for everything Approvals that rubber-stamp every change slow delivery without adding safety. Automate evidence; reserve human approval for high-risk changes. Common mistakeCanary without good metrics If you cannot detect a bad version from metrics, canary analysis passes broken releases. Define SLIs first. Quick check# What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment? Delivery keeps every change releasable with a manual trigger; deployment releases every passing change automatically. Why build once and promote? So the artifact tested is exactly the artifact released; only configuration differs between environments. Blue-green vs canary? Blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments for instant rollback; canary gradually shifts a small share of traffic to the new version and analyses metrics before continuing. What do Argo Rollouts and Flagger do? Automate progressive delivery on Kubernetes: traffic shifting, metric analysis and automatic

b: Simple definition# Kubernetes security is defence in depth across four layers — the 4Cs: Cloud (accounts, networks), Cluster (API access, policies), Container (images, runtime settings) and Code (dependencies, secrets). A weakness in an outer layer undermines everything inside it. The 4Cs of cloud native security flowchart LR subgraph Cloud[&#34;Cloud / data centre&#34;] subgraph Cluster[&#34;Cluster&#34;] subgraph Container[&#34;Container&#34;] Code[&#34;Code&#34;] end end end Security checkpoints on every deployment# kubectl apply to running Pod: security checkpoints · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Authenticate — who is calling? (OIDC users, client certificates, service-account tokens) Authorise — may they do this? (RBAC) Mutating admission — set safe defaults (labels, security context, image digests). Validating admission — reject unsafe specs (Pod Security Admission, Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy in CEL), verify image signatures. Persist to etcd (encrypted at rest). Run with least privilege; runtime detection catches what admission cannot. Identity and access# RBAC grants verbs on resources: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: { name: deployer, namespace: shop } rules: - apiGroups: [&#34;apps&#34;] resources: [&#34;deployments&#34;] verbs: [&#34;get&#34;, &#34;list&#34;, &#34;watch&#34;, &#34;update&#34;, &#34;patch&#34;] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: { name: ci-deployer, namespace: shop } subjects: [{ kind: ServiceAccount, name: argocd-app, namespace: argocd }] roleRef: { kind: Role, name: deployer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io } Humans authenticate through the corporate IdP (OIDC); avoid long-lived kubeconfigs and shared admin accounts. Use Roles in namespaces; reserve ClusterRoles for platform components. Never grant cluster-admin to apps or CI. Service accounts give Pods an identity; tokens are short-lived and audience-bound (projected tokens). Disable automount where not needed. Workload identity (EKS Pod Identity/IRSA, Azure Workload Identity, GKE Workload Identity) maps service accounts to cloud IAM roles — no cloud keys in Secrets. Pod security# Pod Security Standards, enforced by the built-in Pod Security Admission per namespace: Level Meaning Privileged No restrictions (system components only) Baseline Blocks known privilege escalations (host namespaces, privileged containers) Restricted Hardened: non-root, drop all capabilities, no privilege escalation, seccomp RuntimeDefault apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: shop labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted A restricted container spec: securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: { drop: [&#34;ALL&#34;] } seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault } User namespaces (GA in 1.36) map root inside a container to an unprivileged user on the host, reducing the impact of container escapes. Policy as code# Engine Language Notes ValidatingAdmissionPolicy CEL, built in No webhook to run; good for simple rules Kyverno YAML policies Validate, mutate, generate, verify image signatures; CNCF graduated OPA Gatekeeper Rego Very expressive; shared with other OPA use cases Typical rules: required labels and owners, no :latest tags, images only from approved registries and signed, resource requests required, no privileged Pods, Ingress/Route hostnames restricted per team. Secrets# Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded. Enable encryption at rest for etcd (ideally with a KMS provider) and restrict RBAC on Secrets. Prefer an external secret store — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager — synced with the External Secrets Operator or mounted with the Secrets Store CSI driver. Never commit secrets to Git; for GitOps use External Secrets references or encrypted secrets (SOPS, Sealed Secrets). Rotate automatically; prefer short-lived dynamic credentials. Supply-chain security# Secure software supply chain flowchart LR SRC[&#34;Source&lt;br/&gt;signed commits, reviews&#34;] --&gt; BUILD[&#34;Build&lt;br/&gt;hermetic CI, SLSA provenance&#34;] BUILD --&gt; SCAN[&#34;Scan&lt;br/&gt;SCA, SAST, image CVEs&#34;] SCAN --&gt; SBOM[&#34;SBOM&lt;br/&gt;SPDX / CycloneDX&#34;] SBOM --&gt; SIGN[&#34;Sign&lt;br/&gt;cosign / Sigstore&#34;] SIGN --&gt; REG[(&#34;Registry&lt;br/&gt;image + attestations&#34;)] REG --&gt; ADM{&#34;Admission&lt;br/&gt;verify signature,&lt;br/&gt;provenance, policy&#34;} ADM --&gt;|&#34;pass&#34;| RUN[&#34;Run&#34;] ADM --&gt;|&#34;fail&#34;| BLOCK[&#34;Block&#34;] Minimal base images (distroless, Chainguard, Docker Hardened Images, UBI micro) reduce CVEs. SBOMs list every component; SLSA provenance proves how an artifact was built; cosign signs images and attestations; admission policies verify them. Deploy by digest, not tag. Runtime security# Falco or Tetragon (eBPF) detect suspicious behaviour: shells in containers, unexpected network connections, writes to sensitive paths. Restrict egress with NetworkPolicies; audit-log the API server and ship logs to the SIEM. Node hardening: minimal, immutable OS images (Bottlerocket, Talos, Flatcar, RHCOS); auto-patching; no SSH. Multi-tenancy# Model Isolation Use Namespace per team + RBAC + quotas + policies + NetworkPolicies Soft Trusted internal teams Virtual clusters (vCluster) Medium Teams needing their own API/CRDs Dedicated node pools / sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata) Stronger Untrusted or sensitive workloads Separate clusters Hard Regulatory boundaries, very different trust levels Compliance and assessment# CIS Kubernetes Benchmark (kube-bench), NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide, NIST SP 800-190 (container security). Continuous scanning of clusters and manifests (Trivy, Kubescape); policy reports from Kyverno/Gatekeeper. Common mistakes# Common mistakecluster-admin for CI pipelines A compromised pipeline owns

b: Simple definition# GitOps manages infrastructure and applications by keeping their desired state in Git and running agents in the cluster that continuously pull that state and reconcile the cluster to match it. Git becomes the audit log, the review process and the rollback mechanism. The four OpenGitOps principles# Declarative — the system&rsquo;s desired state is expressed declaratively. Versioned and immutable — desired state is stored in a way that keeps full history (Git). Pulled automatically — software agents pull the desired state from the source. Continuously reconciled — agents observe actual state and correct drift. Push vs pull# Push-based CD vs pull-based GitOps flowchart LR subgraph Push[&#34;Push-based&#34;] CI1[&#34;CI pipeline&lt;br/&gt;holds cluster credentials&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;kubectl / helm&#34;| K1[&#34;Cluster&#34;] end subgraph Pull[&#34;Pull-based GitOps&#34;] CI2[&#34;CI pipeline&lt;br/&gt;no cluster credentials&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;PR: new digest&#34;| G[(&#34;Git config repo&#34;)] AG[&#34;Agent in cluster&lt;br/&gt;Argo CD / Flux&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;pull&#34;| G AG --&gt;|&#34;reconcile&#34;| K2[&#34;Cluster&#34;] end Pull wins on security (no cluster credentials outside), drift correction and auditability. The end-to-end flow# GitOps: from pull request to running release · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Argo CD# Argo CD architecture flowchart LR UI[&#34;UI / CLI / API&#34;] --&gt; SRV[&#34;argocd-server&#34;] SRV --&gt; CTRL[&#34;application-controller&lt;br/&gt;compare + sync&#34;] CTRL --&gt; REPO[&#34;repo-server&lt;br/&gt;render Helm, Kustomize, YAML&#34;] REPO --&gt; GIT[(&#34;Git / OCI&#34;)] CTRL --&gt; CL1[&#34;Cluster A&#34;] CTRL --&gt; CL2[&#34;Cluster B&#34;] Application — source (repo, path, chart, revision) + destination (cluster, namespace) + sync policy (auto, prune, self-heal). ApplicationSet — generate many Applications from templates (per cluster, per environment, per Git directory or pull request). App of apps — a parent Application that manages others; useful for bootstrapping clusters. Sync waves and hooks — order resources (CRDs before CRs, migrations before deployments). Projects — RBAC boundaries: which repos, clusters and namespaces a team may use. Argo CD 3.x (2025–2026) tightened RBAC defaults, removed deprecated features and improved ApplicationSet scale; releases arrive roughly quarterly. Flux# A set of controllers (GitOps Toolkit): source-controller (Git, OCI, Helm repos), kustomize-controller, helm-controller, notification-controller, image automation. Fully CRD-driven and CLI-first; native OCI artifact sources; multi-tenancy via namespaced controllers and impersonation. CNCF graduated, like Argo. Argo CD Flux UX Rich UI, visual diff and health CLI/CRDs, UI via add-ons Helm Renders templates (no Helm release objects) Real Helm releases via helm-controller Multi-cluster Central instance managing many clusters, or agents per cluster Usually one Flux per cluster, hub patterns possible Tenancy Projects + RBAC + SSO Namespaced controllers + impersonation Ecosystem Argo Rollouts, Workflows, Events; Kargo for promotion Flagger for progressive delivery Repository structure# platform-config/ # owned by the platform team ├── clusters/ │ ├── prod-eu-1/ # cluster add-ons: ingress/gateway, cert-manager, policies │ └── prod-us-1/ └── applicationsets/ # generate apps per cluster/team team-shop-config/ # owned by the shop team ├── apps/orders/ │ ├── base/ # Kustomize base or Helm values defaults │ └── overlays/ │ ├── dev/ │ ├── staging/ │ └── prod/ # image digest, replicas, resources Separate application source repos from configuration repos (different change rates and permissions). Prefer directories per environment over long-lived branches per environment. Protect production paths with code owners and required reviews. Promotion between environments# CI or a bot (Renovate, Argo CD Image Updater, Flux image automation) opens a PR to bump the image digest in dev. After tests pass, promotion to staging/prod is another PR (manual or automated). Kargo (from the Argo ecosystem) and release orchestrators such as Digital.ai Release manage multi-stage promotion with verification and approvals. Secrets in GitOps# Never store plaintext secrets in Git. Options: Option How External Secrets Operator Git stores a reference; the operator fetches from Vault/cloud secret managers Sealed Secrets Encrypt with the cluster&rsquo;s public key; only the controller decrypts SOPS Encrypt values with KMS/age; Flux/Argo plugins decrypt Drift and self-healing# Detect drift: someone runs kubectl edit in production → the app shows OutOfSync. Self-heal: the controller reverts the change automatically. Allow intentional runtime changes (HPA replica counts, injected fields) with ignoreDifferences rules. Common mistakes# Common mistakeBranch per environment Merges between long-lived branches drift and conflict. Use folders/overlays per environment on one main branch. Common mistakeGitOps for everything, including secrets in plain text Use external secret references or encryption. Common mistakeOne Argo CD admin for all teams Use Projects, SSO groups and least-privilege destinations so teams manage only their own apps. Quick check# What are the OpenGitOps principles? Declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled. Why is pull-based deployment more secure? CI never holds cluster credentials; the in-cluster agent pulls from Git, and every change is a reviewed commit. What is an ApplicationSet? An Argo CD resource that generates Applications from templates and generators (clusters, Git directories, lists, pull requests) — ideal for fleets and many teams. b: Simple definition# Release orchestration coordinates everything that has to happen for a release across many teams, tools and environments: builds, deployments, tests, security checks, approvals, change tickets, communications and evidence for auditors. CI/CD and GitOps automate a pipeline; release orchestration automates the release process around many pipelines. Digital.ai Release (formerly XebiaLabs XL Release) is a release orchestration platform; Digital.ai Deploy (formerly XL Deploy) is a model-driven deployment automation tool. They are part of the wider Digital.ai platform, which also includes agile planning, continuous testing and application security products. Why enterprises add an orchestration layer# Challenge in large organisations What orchestration adds A release spans 20 services, a mainframe and a database change One release plan coordinating all of them Many tools: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Argo CD, ServiceNow, Jira, test tools Integrations and a single view Regulated change management (CAB, segregation of duties) Automated approvals, gates, audit trail, evidence Different deployment targets: Kubernetes, VMs, cloud, packaged apps Model-driven deployment and plug-ins Visibility for management Dashboards, release calendars, risk scores, DORA-style metrics Release orchestration in the delivery flow# Orchestrated release: CI, gates and GitOps deployment · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ CI builds, tests, scans and signs the artifact once. The release orchestrator runs the release template: deploys to test (through Argo CD or Deploy), collects test and security results, evaluates quality gates and a risk score. Change approval is automatic for low-risk changes or routed to a CAB/ServiceNow change for high-risk ones. Production deployment runs through GitOps and progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts canary). Analysis promotes or triggers an automatic rollback; every step is recorded for audit. Core concepts in Digital.ai Release# Concept Meaning Template A reusable release blueprint (for example &ldquo;Monthly payments platform release&rdquo;) Release A running instance of a template, with its own variables and timeline Phase A stage of the release: Build, Test, Approve, Deploy to production, Verify Task A unit of work: automated (call Jenkins, sync Argo CD, create ServiceNow change, run tests) or manual (sign-off) Gate A checkpoint that blocks progress until conditions are met (tests passed, approvals given, dependencies released) Variables Values passed between tasks (version, image digest, change ticket number) Folders and teams Organise templates and permissions per business unit Triggers Start releases from events (new artifact, Git tag, deployment event) Dashboards, Release Calendar, Risk profile Portfolio view, blackout windows, risk scoring A release template flowchart LR P1[&#34;Phase: Build&lt;br/&gt;Jenkins / GitHub Actions task&#34;] --&gt; P2[&#34;Phase: Test&lt;br/&gt;Argo CD sync to test&lt;br/&gt;+ automated test tasks&#34;] P2 --&gt; G1{&#34;Gate: quality&lt;br/&gt;tests ≥ threshold,&lt;br/&gt;no critical CVEs&#34;} G1 --&gt; P3[&#34;Phase: Approve&lt;br/&gt;ServiceNow change&lt;br/&gt;(auto if low risk)&#34;] P3 --&gt; P4[&#34;Phase: Production&lt;br/&gt;Argo Rollouts canary&#34;] P4 --&gt; P5[&#34;Phase: Verify&lt;br/&gt;SLO checks, notify&#34;] Cloud native integrations# Recent Digital.ai Release versions (26.x, 2026) emphasise Kubernetes and GitOps: Argo CD plugin — sync, wait for health, roll back, terminate a running operation, and manage ignoreDifferences rules from release tasks; onboarding workflows to create Argo CD Applications. Argo Rollouts plugin — drive blue-green and canary rollouts and promotions as release tasks. Flux CD and Tekton container-based plugins. Live Deployments — a single view of what is deployed where, whether deployed by Release, Deploy, Argo CD or Flux; deployment events can trigger releases. Digital.ai Deploy GitOps — exchange infrastructure and environment configuration items with Git as YAML. Integrations with Jenkins, GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Jira, ServiceNow, test and security tools; a Release MCP server (beta) for AI assistants. Digital.ai Deploy (model-driven deployment)# Deploy describes what to deploy (a versioned deployment package of artifacts and resources) and where (environments of infrastructure items); it calculates the steps (create, modify, destroy) and runs them with rollback. It is valuable for non-Kubernetes targets — application servers, VMs, databases, mainframe-adjacent systems — which are still common in banks and insurers. For Kubernetes, GitOps tools usually perform the deployment, orchestrated by Release. Deployment models# SaaS or self-hosted (including on Kubernetes via an operator). Remote runners execute container-based tasks close to target environments. When to use release orchestration# Use it when: many teams release interdependent changes; regulated change management requires evidence and approvals; you deploy to a mix of Kubernetes and legacy targets; leadership needs portfolio-level release visibility. You may not need it when: teams deploy independent microservices continuously with GitOps and automated gates, and audit needs are met by Git history and pipeline evidence. Alternatives and complements# Tool Notes Kargo Open-source, GitOps-native multi-stage promotion Harness, Octopus Deploy, CloudBees Commercial CD/release platforms Spinnaker Open-source multi-cloud CD (heavier to operate) GitLab / GitHub environments + deployment protection rules Built-in approvals and environment gates ServiceNow DevOps Change Change automation tied to pipelines Common mistakes# Common mistakeOrchestration that re-implements CI The orchestrator should call CI and GitOps, not replace them. Keep build logic in CI and deployment in GitOps. Common mistakeEvery release through a manual CAB Use risk scoring and automated evidence so low-risk changes are
